guides.title: How a Computer Works: Bits, Logic Gates & the CPU
guides.summary: From a single on/off switch to a working processor: how bits and binary numbers, Boolean logic gates, adders and memory cells, and the fetch-decode-execute cycle combine to turn electricity into computation.

sections.heading: Bits, Bytes and Binary Numbers
sections.body:
A computer stores and manipulates information as bits. A bit, short for binary digit, is the smallest unit of data and holds exactly one of two values, written 0 or 1. Physically a bit is a voltage level on a wire or the charge state of a tiny capacitor: a voltage near ground counts as 0 and a voltage near the supply rail counts as 1. The reason for using only two states rather than ten is noise immunity. Real circuits pick up interference from neighbouring wires, temperature drift and power-supply ripple, and a design that only has to distinguish "near 0 volts" from "near 1 volt" tolerates far more of that corruption than one trying to distinguish ten levels a tenth of a volt apart. Every gate along the way restores a degraded signal to a clean full-rail value, so a bit can pass through a billion stages without accumulating error.

Bits are grouped for convenience. Eight bits make one byte, which can represent 2^8 = 256 distinct values, conventionally 0 to 255. Numbers are stored in base two rather than base ten. In base two each digit position is a power of two, so reading right to left the place values are 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64 and 128. To convert a binary number to decimal, multiply each bit by its place value and add: binary 1011 is 1×8 + 0×4 + 1×2 + 1×1 = 11. To convert the other way, divide repeatedly by two and read the remainders from bottom to top. Thirteen divided by two is six remainder 1; six divided by two is three remainder 0; three divided by two is one remainder 1; one divided by two is zero remainder 1 — giving 1101.

Several groupings recur. Four bits are a nibble, which maps exactly onto one hexadecimal digit from 0 to F, which is why hexadecimal is used to write out raw memory: two hex characters express one byte compactly and unambiguously. A word is the natural operating width of a given processor, 32 or 64 bits on most modern machines.

Storage prefixes are a genuine and persistent source of confusion. A kilobyte in the decimal sense is 1,000 bytes, while a kibibyte is 2^10 = 1,024 bytes, and the same split applies to megabyte against mebibyte and gigabyte against gibibyte. Drive manufacturers advertise in decimal units and most operating systems report in binary ones, which is the entire reason a drive sold as one terabyte shows up as roughly 931 gibibytes. Nothing is missing; the two numbers are the same quantity in different units. Network speeds add a further trap by being quoted in bits per second rather than bytes, so a connection advertised at 100 megabits delivers at best about 12.5 megabytes each second.

sections.heading: Boolean Logic and the Fundamental Gates
sections.body:
All computation reduces to Boolean algebra, the system George Boole set out in his 1854 work An Investigation of the Laws of Thought, which operates on just two values, TRUE written as 1 and FALSE written as 0. Boole was doing philosophy of logic and had no machine in mind. The connection to hardware came in 1937, when Claude Shannon showed in his master's thesis at MIT that networks of electrical relays implement exactly Boolean expressions — arguably the single most consequential master's thesis ever written, because it turned circuit design from craft into algebra.

A logic gate is a physical circuit, built from transistors, that computes one Boolean function of its inputs. Six matter. NOT, also called an inverter, takes one input and produces its opposite, so NOT 0 is 1 and NOT 1 is 0. AND produces 1 only when every input is 1. OR produces 1 when at least one input is 1. XOR, exclusive OR, produces 1 when its inputs differ, which makes it the core of binary addition, since adding two bits gives a 1 in the ones column precisely when the inputs are not the same. NAND and NOR are AND and OR with the output inverted.

NAND deserves particular attention because it is functionally complete, or universal: every other gate can be built from NAND gates alone. An inverter is a NAND with both inputs tied together. An AND is a NAND followed by that inverter. An OR is a NAND fed by two inverted inputs, which follows from De Morgan's laws — the identities stating that NOT (A AND B) equals (NOT A) OR (NOT B), and NOT (A OR B) equals (NOT A) AND (NOT B). NOR is universal in the same way. This matters commercially as well as theoretically: a fabrication process that produces one highly optimised gate type can build an entire processor from it, and in CMOS technology NAND happens to be cheaper and faster to implement than AND.

A truth table lists every possible input combination alongside the resulting output, and is the standard way to specify or verify a circuit. A gate with n inputs needs 2^n rows, so a two-input gate has four rows and a three-input gate has eight. That exponential growth is why truth tables are used for small blocks and algebraic simplification for anything larger. Gates are the entire vocabulary of hardware. A modern processor is hundreds of millions to tens of billions of these six functions wired together, and nothing else.

One further property is worth stating plainly, because it is what licenses the whole discipline: any function from bits to bits, no matter how complicated, can be written as a Boolean expression and therefore built from gates. There is no operation a computer performs that requires anything beyond this vocabulary — only more of it, arranged more cleverly.

sections.heading: From Gates to Arithmetic: the Adder
sections.body:
Adding two single bits produces two output bits, because 1 plus 1 is binary 10 — a sum of 0 with a carry of 1. A circuit that computes both is called a half adder, and it needs exactly two gates: the sum is A XOR B, and the carry is A AND B. Checking the four cases confirms it. Zero plus zero gives XOR 0 and AND 0, so 00. Zero plus one and one plus zero each give XOR 1 and AND 0, so 01. One plus one gives XOR 0 and AND 1, so 10, which is decimal 2. Two gates perform arithmetic.

A half adder cannot be chained, because it has no way to receive a carry from the column to its right. A full adder fixes this by accepting a third input, the carry-in, and is built from two half adders plus an OR gate. Its sum is A XOR B XOR Cin, and its carry-out is (A AND B) OR (Cin AND (A XOR B)) — in words, a carry is generated either when both input bits are 1, or when exactly one of them is 1 and a carry arrived from the previous column.

Placing n full adders side by side, with each stage's carry-out wired into the next stage's carry-in, yields a ripple-carry adder that adds two n-bit numbers. This is literally how the arithmetic-logic unit inside a processor adds integers. The name describes its main weakness: the carry must physically propagate from the lowest bit to the highest, so a 64-bit ripple-carry adder has a worst-case delay of 64 gate stages. Real processors therefore use carry-lookahead or carry-select designs, which compute in parallel whether each column will generate or propagate a carry and so reduce the delay from proportional to n down to roughly proportional to the logarithm of n, at the cost of considerably more gates.

Subtraction needs no new hardware at all, thanks to two's complement representation. To compute A minus B, invert every bit of B and add 1, then feed that into the same adder. In an n-bit two's complement system the leading bit indicates sign, the representable range is −2^(n−1) to 2^(n−1) − 1, and there is exactly one zero — an asymmetry that leaves one extra negative value with no positive counterpart. Multiplication is repeated shift-and-add, division repeated subtract-and-shift. The essential point is that AND, OR, XOR and NOT are sufficient to construct every arithmetic operation a computer performs.

Two's complement is worth appreciating rather than merely memorising, because it is why one adder suffices. Under it, negative numbers are represented such that adding a value to its negation naturally overflows to zero within the fixed width, so the hardware never needs to know or care which operand is negative. The alternative schemes tried in early machines — sign-and-magnitude, and ones' complement — both produced two distinct representations of zero and needed extra correction logic, and both were abandoned for exactly that reason.

sections.heading: Remembering a Bit: Latches, Flip-Flops and Registers
sections.body:
Gates on their own are combinational, meaning the output depends only on the inputs present right now. Remove the inputs and the output vanishes; there is no memory anywhere in such a circuit. Storage requires feedback — routing an output back around to an input so the circuit can hold itself in a state.

Cross-coupling two NOR gates, with each gate's output feeding one input of the other, produces an SR latch. Asserting the Set input drives the stored bit to 1, asserting Reset drives it to 0, and with both inputs low the loop sustains whatever value it currently holds indefinitely, each gate continuously reasserting the condition that keeps the other in place. The latch has one genuine flaw worth knowing: asserting Set and Reset simultaneously drives both outputs low, violating the normal invariant that they are complementary, and releasing both at once leaves the final state determined by which gate happens to be marginally faster. That is why raw SR latches are rarely exposed directly in a design.

Adding a clock input produces a D latch, which is transparent — passing its data input straight through — while the clock is high, and frozen while it is low. Refining that into an edge-triggered D flip-flop, usually by chaining two latches driven from opposite clock phases, gives the component modern synchronous design is built on: it samples its data input only at the instant of a clock edge and holds the captured value untouched until the next edge. That single behaviour is what makes a complex machine analysable, because every storage element in the design updates at the same predictable moment.

Edge triggering imposes timing rules. Setup time is the interval before the clock edge during which the data input must already be stable; hold time is the interval after it during which the data must not change. Violating either can drive the flip-flop into metastability, an unstable balanced state where the output hovers between valid levels for an unpredictable period. Metastability cannot be eliminated, only made arbitrarily improbable, which is why signals crossing between independent clock domains pass through synchroniser chains.

A register is simply a row of flip-flops sharing a clock — sixty-four of them to hold one machine word. Processors have a small set of named registers used as the fastest possible scratchpads. Main memory takes a different approach: static RAM stores each bit in a six-transistor latch, fast but expensive in area, while dynamic RAM stores each bit as charge on a single tiny capacitor guarded by one transistor. That charge leaks away within tens of milliseconds, so every row must be read and rewritten thousands of times per second — the refresh that gives dynamic RAM its name, and the reason it is dense and cheap but slower.

sections.heading: The CPU and the Fetch-Decode-Execute Cycle
sections.body:
The central processing unit runs a program — a list of very simple instructions stored in memory — by repeating one loop billions of times per second. In the fetch step, a register called the program counter holds the memory address of the next instruction, and the processor copies the bits at that address into the instruction register. In the decode step, the control unit interprets that bit pattern, splitting off an opcode identifying the operation and operand fields identifying which registers or addresses it applies to, then raises the internal control signals that configure the rest of the chip. In the execute step, the arithmetic-logic unit or another functional unit performs the work: adding, comparing, moving data, or changing the flow of control. Finally the result is written back to a register or to memory, and the program counter advances to the following instruction — unless the instruction was a jump or branch, in which case the counter is loaded with a new address instead. Conditional branching is what makes the machine general-purpose rather than a calculator; without it there are no loops and no decisions.

This organisation is the von Neumann architecture, named for the 1945 First Draft of a Report on the EDVAC, whose defining feature is that instructions and data share one memory. The consequence is that a program can treat its own instructions as data — the basis of compilers, loaders and self-modifying code, and also of a whole family of security vulnerabilities. The alternative Harvard architecture keeps instruction and data memories separate and survives in microcontrollers and in the split instruction and data caches of otherwise von Neumann processors. The particular repertoire of instructions a processor recognises is its instruction set architecture, such as x86-64, ARM or RISC-V.

The plain four-step loop describes almost no modern processor accurately. Pipelining overlaps the stages of consecutive instructions like an assembly line, so that while one instruction executes, the next is being decoded and a third fetched; a pipeline of depth k can approach k times the throughput without the clock running any faster. That gain is threatened by hazards — an instruction needing a result not yet written back, or a branch whose direction is unknown when the next fetch must already happen. Processors answer with forwarding paths, branch prediction that guesses and speculatively executes ahead, superscalar issue of several instructions per cycle, and out-of-order execution that reorders work while preserving the appearance of sequential order. Multiple cores add genuinely independent processors on one chip. Every one of these is an optimisation over the same underlying loop, not a replacement for it. Speculative execution in particular turned out to have consequences nobody anticipated: the Spectre and Meltdown vulnerabilities disclosed in 2018 exploited traces left in the cache by speculatively executed work that was subsequently discarded, showing that a performance optimisation invisible at the instruction level can still be observable.

sections.heading: Buses, the Memory Hierarchy and the Clock
sections.body:
Components communicate over buses, which are shared bundles of parallel wires with agreed meanings. The address bus carries which memory location is wanted, its width setting the maximum addressable space — 32 address lines reach 4 gibibytes, 64 reach far more than any machine has. The data bus carries the bits themselves, and the control bus carries the signals saying whether this is a read or a write and when the values are valid. Modern high-speed links have largely replaced wide parallel buses with narrow serial lanes, because at gigahertz rates the individual wires of a wide bus no longer arrive in step with one another, but the logical division of address, data and control persists.

Fast memory is expensive and slow memory is cheap, so machines arrange storage in a hierarchy and rely on locality of reference — the empirical observation that programs reuse recently touched data and tend to access neighbouring addresses. Registers sit at the top, perhaps a kilobyte in total, available within a single cycle. L1 cache holds tens of kilobytes at roughly four cycles. L2 and L3 caches hold hundreds of kilobytes to tens of megabytes at roughly twelve to forty cycles. Main dynamic RAM holds many gigabytes at something like 200 to 300 cycles, which is around 60 to 100 nanoseconds. Solid-state storage holds hundreds of gigabytes to terabytes at tens of microseconds, and a spinning hard disk at several milliseconds — the last of which, in cycle terms, is comparable to tens of millions of cycles.

Caches move data in fixed blocks called cache lines, typically 64 bytes, which is why walking an array in order is dramatically faster than jumping about at random: sequential access gets seven or more useful values per line fetched, while random access wastes most of each. Understanding that single fact explains a large fraction of real-world performance differences between algorithms with identical theoretical complexity.

Everything is paced by the clock, generated by a quartz crystal oscillator and multiplied up by a phase-locked loop to the processor's operating frequency. A 3 GHz clock ticks three billion times per second, giving a period of about 0.33 nanoseconds. On each tick every synchronised flip-flop simultaneously captures its new value, so the clock is the metronome keeping billions of gates in lockstep. The period sets a hard budget: all the combinational logic between one flip-flop and the next must settle within it, or the captured value will be wrong. Light itself travels only about ten centimetres in 0.33 nanoseconds, and signals in copper travel slower still, which is one of the physical reasons clock speeds stopped climbing in the mid-2000s and designers turned to more cores instead.

sections.heading: Worked Example: Adding 5 + 3 Inside the Machine
sections.body:
Following a single addition all the way down shows that nothing along the path is mysterious. Suppose a short program says: load 5, load 3, add them, store the result. Assume a four-bit machine for readability; a real one works identically with sixty-four columns instead of four.

First the values are represented. Decimal 5 is binary 0101, because 4 + 1 = 5. Decimal 3 is binary 0011, because 2 + 1 = 3.

Next the loads. The program counter holds the address of the first instruction, and the processor copies the bits at that address into the instruction register. The control unit decodes the opcode as a load, reads the operand fields to learn the destination register and the source value, and raises the control signals that gate 0101 onto the internal bus and into register R1. On the next clock edge the flip-flops making up R1 capture it and hold it. The program counter advances and the process repeats, putting 0011 into R2.

Now the addition. Both registers are routed to the inputs of the arithmetic-logic unit's adder, and four full adders work the columns from right to left, each computing sum as A XOR B XOR carry-in and carry-out as (A AND B) OR (carry-in AND (A XOR B)). In the ones column, 1 plus 1 with no carry-in gives sum 0 and carry 1. In the twos column, 0 plus 1 plus the incoming carry of 1 gives sum 0 and carry 1. In the fours column, 1 plus 0 plus carry 1 gives sum 0 and carry 1. In the eights column, 0 plus 0 plus carry 1 gives sum 1 and carry 0. Reading the sum bits from the top column down gives 1000, which is decimal 8. Correct.

Two details are worth noticing. The carries rippled through all four columns in sequence, so the result was not valid until the last one settled — the clock period must be long enough to cover that whole chain. And the final carry-out being 0 is what tells the machine no overflow occurred; had the operands been 12 and 5, the four-bit result would have wrapped to 1 with a carry-out of 1, and it is entirely the program's responsibility to check.

Finally the write-back stores 1000 into a register or memory location and the program counter advances. The whole sequence takes a handful of clock cycles, comfortably under a billionth of a second, and consists only of voltages, gates and a clock repeating the same disciplined loop.

On a real processor the same trace would be complicated by the loads probably hitting cache rather than memory, by the two loads and the add being in flight simultaneously in different pipeline stages, and by the adder being a carry-lookahead design rather than a ripple chain. None of that changes the arithmetic or the result. It only changes how many of these operations finish per second.

sections.heading: Common Misconceptions and Practical Notes
sections.body:
Computers do not understand code. A processor responds to bit patterns and nothing else; the words in a programming language exist entirely for humans. A compiler or interpreter translates that text down into machine instructions, and by the time anything executes, the names, comments and structure are gone. This is why a syntax error is caught before the program runs while a logic error is not: the translator can check that the text is well-formed, but the hardware has no notion of what you intended.

More gigahertz does not simply mean faster. Clock speed is one term in a product that also includes instructions completed per cycle, core count, cache size and memory bandwidth. A modern 3 GHz processor vastly outperforms a fifteen-year-old 3 GHz processor at the same nominal frequency, because it retires several instructions per cycle instead of one and misses cache far less often. Comparing frequencies across different designs tells you almost nothing.

RAM and storage are not the same thing. Dynamic RAM is fast, volatile working memory that loses everything when power is removed; solid-state drives and hard disks are far slower but persistent. Programs execute out of RAM and are saved to storage, which is why an unsaved document disappears in a power cut and why adding RAM helps a machine that is swapping while adding storage does not.

A bit is never blank. It is always exactly one of two states, and there is no third empty condition. A memory cell that has never been written still holds some value; it is simply an arbitrary one.

More cores do not make one program faster. A single-threaded task uses one core no matter how many exist, and even a parallelised program is bounded by Amdahl's law: if a tenth of the work is inherently sequential, no number of cores can give more than roughly a tenfold speedup.

Several practical points follow from the physics. Chips throttle their clock when they overheat, so cooling and thermal paste have real performance consequences rather than merely extending lifespan. Error-correcting memory adds extra bits per word so that a single flipped bit — caused by cosmic rays, electrical noise or a marginal cell — is detected and repaired transparently, which matters for servers running for years. And the same binary logic scales unchanged from a one-dollar microcontroller to a supercomputer; only the number of gates, cores and memory channels differs.

One last point cuts across all of these. Deleting a file usually removes only its directory entry, leaving the actual bytes on the drive until something else overwrites them, which is why deleted data is often recoverable and why securely erasing a drive is a separate operation. Understanding this bottom layer is what demystifies everything above it, from operating systems to applications, because at every level the machinery turns out to be the same handful of ideas repeated at a larger scale.

sections.heading: Transistors: The Physical Switch Behind Every Gate
sections.body:
Every AND, OR and NOT is an abstraction resting on one physical device: the transistor. Modern chips are built from the MOSFET, the metal-oxide-semiconductor field-effect transistor, a three-terminal switch with a source, a drain and a gate. Apply a voltage above a threshold to the gate and the electric field it creates pulls charge carriers into a thin channel beneath the insulating oxide, connecting source to drain and letting current flow — the transistor turns on. Drop the gate voltage below that threshold and the channel disappears — it turns off. That is the whole physical basis of 1s and 0s: a voltage near the supply rail is a logical 1, a voltage near ground is a logical 0, and the transistor is a voltage-controlled valve deciding which one appears at the output. Crucially the gate is insulated from the channel, so controlling the switch costs essentially no steady current, only the energy to charge and discharge a tiny capacitance.

Real circuits pair two flavours of this switch: an NMOS transistor that conducts when its gate is high, and a PMOS transistor that conducts when its gate is low. Wiring one of each so that exactly one is on for any input, and never both, is CMOS — complementary MOS — the technology behind essentially every processor since the 1980s. Because there is no path from supply to ground while the output sits steady, meaningful current flows only during the brief switching transition. That is why power consumption scales with how often gates change state rather than with how many exist, and why a chip with billions of transistors can sit in a phone rather than needing industrial cooling. A CMOS inverter takes two transistors, a NAND takes four, and a flip-flop a few dozen.

The transistor was demonstrated at Bell Labs in December 1947 by John Bardeen and Walter Brattain, with William Shockley developing the more manufacturable junction transistor shortly after; the three shared the 1956 Nobel Prize in Physics. It replaced the vacuum tube, a fragile, power-hungry glass bulb doing the same switching job at roughly a hundred times the size, with a lifespan measured in months. ENIAC, completed in 1945, used about 17,468 tubes and kept technicians on standby because tubes failed constantly.

Intel's 4004 of 1971, the first commercial microprocessor, packed 2,300 transistors onto one die; a current phone or laptop processor packs tens of billions onto a chip smaller than a fingernail. That doubling of density roughly every two years is what Gordon Moore observed in 1965. The honest caveat is that modern process names such as "3 nm" are marketing labels rather than any measured physical dimension, and that the accompanying power-scaling relationship broke down around 2005 — which is precisely why clock speeds plateaued and core counts rose instead.

sections.heading: Instruction Sets: How Software Becomes Electricity
sections.body:
An instruction, seen from the hardware, is just a binary number carved into fields. The set of numbers a given processor recognises, and what each one means, is its instruction set architecture — the fixed contract every compiler and assembler must target, and the boundary between everything written in software and everything etched in silicon. Two processors sharing an ISA run the same binaries however differently they are built internally, which is exactly why a program compiled in 2005 still runs today.

RISC-V, an open and royalty-free ISA used in embedded chips and increasingly in general-purpose machines, shows the structure clearly because its base instructions are a uniform 32 bits. An add instruction, written add rd, rs1, rs2 and meaning put the sum of rs1 and rs2 into rd, is laid out as a 7-bit opcode in the lowest bits, a 5-bit destination register field, a 3-bit function code, two 5-bit source register fields, and a 7-bit function extension at the top. Five bits address a register because the architecture has 32 of them. When that word reaches the control unit during decode, hard-wired logic reads those fields and raises precisely the control signals that route the two named registers into the adder inputs and steer the sum back to the destination — the abstraction of an instruction cashes out as specific wires going high or low. Fixed width is what makes decoding cheap: the processor always knows where the next instruction begins.

x86-64, the ISA in most desktop and laptop processors, is the opposite. Its instructions run from 1 to 15 bytes, because the design grew by accretion from 1978 onward, layering new capabilities onto an old encoding for the sake of backward compatibility. Finding where one instruction ends requires partially decoding it, which makes parallel decode genuinely hard. This is the enduring RISC versus CISC split — reduced, fixed-width and simple against complex, variable-width and feature-rich. The practical resolution is untidy: modern x86 processors decode those complex instructions into simple internal micro-operations and execute those, so the RISC ideas won inside the chip while the CISC interface survived outside it.

Almost none of this is written by hand. A compiler for C or Rust, or a runtime for Java or Python, translates source through several layers, typically producing assembly language — a human-readable one-to-one stand-in for machine instructions, with mnemonics like mov, add and jmp — which an assembler then converts into raw opcodes. Every application, however sophisticated, bottoms out in a stream of words the decoder splits into fields, billions of times a second. This is also why a program compiled for one architecture will not run on another without either recompilation from source or emulation that translates instructions at runtime, and why the industry's periodic architecture migrations are such large undertakings.

sections.heading: Equipment You'll Actually Need
sections.body:
None of this requires a professional lab. A basic hobby-electronics bench is enough to build and probe real logic gates by hand rather than only simulating them, and the total outlay is modest — the gate chips themselves cost well under a pound or dollar each.

A solderless breadboard is the foundation. Its rows of spring clips connect components without soldering, so a circuit can be rewired repeatedly while learning. The layout follows a fixed convention: two long rails down each side for power and ground, and short five-hole columns in the middle, split by a central channel sized so that a dual-in-line chip straddles it with each pin landing in its own column.

The gate chips come from two families that look interchangeable and are not. The original 7400 series is bipolar TTL, tolerant of sloppy wiring and forgiving of unconnected inputs, which float to a logical 1. The 74HC series is CMOS: it draws far less current, works over a wider supply range, and is much less forgiving, because an unconnected input is genuinely undefined and will drift, oscillate and waste power. If using 74HC parts, every unused input needs tying to ground or to the supply through a resistor. This one detail causes most of the mystifying behaviour beginners encounter.

Power should be a clean, regulated 5 volts. A benchtop supply with a current limit is ideal because it protects the circuit from a wiring mistake, but four AA cells through a regulator work. Note that batteries sag under load and a fresh alkaline pack can exceed 6 volts, which is outside the safe range for some parts.

Indicator LEDs must never be connected directly across the supply, since a diode has no meaningful resistance once conducting and will destroy itself or the driving output. The series resistor sets the current: with a 5-volt rail, a red LED dropping about 2 volts, and a 220-ohm resistor, Ohm's law gives roughly 13.6 milliamps, comfortably within both the LED's rating and a logic chip's output capability. Larger resistors simply give a dimmer but perfectly readable indication.

A multimeter turns guesswork into measurement, letting you confirm the supply is really at the pins and read the actual voltage at an output rather than inferring it from a lamp.
ingredients: A solderless breadboard (an inexpensive reusable prototyping board, sold at any electronics/hobby store)

A handful of basic logic-gate ICs from the 7400-series (e.g. a 7408 AND, 7432 OR, 7404 NOT, 7486 XOR) or the 74HC00-series CMOS equivalents — sold individually and cheaply at any electronics/hobby store
Assorted jumper wires (male-to-male breadboard wires, sold in packs)
A simple 5V power source — a small benchtop power supply, or a battery pack (e.g. 4 AA batteries in a holder) with a basic voltage regulator or current-limiting resistor
A few 5mm LEDs plus matching 220-330 ohm resistors, wired as simple on/off output indicators
A digital multimeter (any basic $15-30 model with voltage and continuity testing) to verify what's actually happening at each pin
Optional: a free online logic-circuit simulator, useful for planning a circuit or checking your truth table before wiring anything physically

sections.heading: Step-by-Step: Build and Test a Half-Adder Yourself
sections.body:
A half adder is small enough to breadboard in under an hour and gives a physical demonstration that binary addition is nothing more than two gates switching. It takes two input bits and produces two outputs — a Sum, which is the exclusive-OR of the inputs, and a Carry, which is their AND. Wiring exactly that and watching two LEDs reproduce the addition table is a genuinely different experience from reading the truth table.

A few points explain why the procedure runs the way it does. The two input wires feed both chips at once because a half adder computes both functions of the same pair of bits simultaneously; there is no sequence and no ordering. Inputs must be tied firmly to the supply rail or to ground rather than left dangling, since a floating input on a CMOS part is undefined and will produce results that appear random and change when you move your hand near the board. The resistor in series with each LED limits current to a safe value and is not optional. Power and ground go to specific pins fixed by the package — on a standard 14-pin logic chip that is pin 14 for the supply and pin 7 for ground — and getting them backwards will destroy the part immediately.

If an output stays stubbornly dark or lit, check the supply voltage at the chip's own pins with a meter before suspecting the logic. Loose breadboard contacts and a rail that was never actually connected account for the large majority of failures.
steps: Get one XOR gate IC and one AND gate IC (e.g. a 7486 and a 7408), each providing four independent 2-input gates per chip.
Check the chip's pinout diagram (printed on the packaging or easily looked up from the part number) and wire pin 14 to your +5V rail and pin 7 to ground on each chip.
Wire two jumper wires as inputs A and B, each switchable between +5V (logic 1) and ground (logic 0).
Feed A and B into both the first XOR gate's two inputs and the first AND gate's two inputs simultaneously (both chips read the same two input wires).
Connect the XOR gate's output through a 220-330 ohm resistor to an LED — this is your Sum output.
Connect the AND gate's output through a second resistor to a second LED — this is your Carry output.
Test all four input combinations in turn — (A=0,B=0), (0,1), (1,0), (1,1) — noting which LEDs light for each.
Compare your results against binary addition by hand: 0+0=00, 0+1=01, 1+0=01, 1+1=10 — the Sum LED should track the ones-place bit and the Carry LED the twos-place bit exactly.

Extension: wire a second half-adder plus an OR gate to combine their carry outputs, producing a full adder with a carry-in, and verify it correctly computes 1+1+1=11 (decimal 3) — the same block chained together seven more times becomes the 8-bit adder inside a real, simple CPU.

guides.title: Algorithms & Thinking Like a Programmer
guides.summary: What an algorithm is, how to measure its efficiency with Big-O notation, the core control structures and data structures, and a repeatable method for decomposing any problem into a correct, testable solution — with worked search and sort examples.

sections.heading: What an Algorithm Is
sections.body:
An algorithm is a finite, precise sequence of unambiguous steps that transforms an input into a desired output and that is guaranteed to stop. The word descends from the ninth-century Persian scholar Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi, whose treatise on systematic calculation reached medieval Europe under the Latinized form of his name, Algoritmi; the same book gave us the word algebra. The concept, though, is far older than the word and far broader than computers: long division, the Euclidean method for finding a greatest common divisor, and the procedure for balancing a chequebook are all algorithms, and none of them requires electricity.

Five formal properties, set out in this form by Donald Knuth, separate an algorithm from a vague procedure. Finiteness means it terminates after a bounded number of steps rather than running forever. Definiteness means each step is specified exactly, with no room for interpretation. Input means it takes zero or more well-defined values to start from. Output means it produces one or more values standing in a stated relationship to the input. Effectiveness means every step is basic enough that a person could in principle carry it out with pencil and paper. A recipe is the usual analogy and it is a useful one, but recipes routinely violate definiteness: an instruction to add salt to taste is not an algorithmic step, whereas adding five grams of salt is.

Correctness is a stronger claim than the code appearing to work. An algorithm is correct if it produces the right output for every valid input, which is not something a handful of passing examples can establish. Two formal tools do most of the work here. A loop invariant is a condition that holds before the loop starts, remains true after each iteration, and, combined with the loop's exit condition, implies the desired result. For a loop that scans a list tracking the largest value seen, the invariant is that the tracked value is the maximum of everything examined so far; when the scan finishes, everything has been examined, so the tracked value is the maximum overall. Mathematical induction serves the same role for recursive definitions. Proving termination is a separate obligation, usually met by identifying a quantity that strictly decreases with each step and cannot decrease forever.

Determinism means the same input always drives the same steps and yields the same output. Some algorithms deliberately abandon this and make random choices, either to avoid a worst case an adversary could construct, as randomized quicksort does when picking its pivot, or to obtain speed at the cost of a tiny, quantifiable probability of error, as the Miller-Rabin primality test does. Finally, it is worth knowing that not every well-posed problem has an algorithm at all: Alan Turing proved in 1936 that no procedure can decide, for every possible program and input, whether that program will eventually halt.

sections.heading: Measuring Efficiency: Big-O Notation
sections.body:
Two algorithms can both be correct and still differ enormously in cost, so the discipline needs a way to compare them that does not depend on which laptop happened to run the test. Big-O notation provides it by describing how the number of basic operations grows as the input size n grows, deliberately discarding constant factors and lower-order terms. Formally, a function f(n) is O(g(n)) if there exist a constant c greater than zero and a size n-nought such that f(n) is at most c times g(n) for every n beyond n-nought. Dropping constants sounds like throwing away information, and it is, but it is exactly the information that varies with processor speed, language, and compiler, leaving behind the part that belongs to the algorithm itself.

The growth classes worth memorizing, from best to worst, run as follows. Constant time, written O(1), means the cost does not depend on n at all, as when reading an array element by its index. Logarithmic time, O(log n), arises when each step halves the remaining problem; because the logarithm base two of one million is about twenty, a logarithmic algorithm on a million items does roughly twenty steps. Linear time, O(n), means one pass over the data. Linearithmic time, O(n log n), is the provable lower bound for any sorting method that works by comparing pairs of elements, and is achieved by merge sort and by quicksort on average. Quadratic time, O(n squared), arises from a loop nested inside another loop over the same data; for a thousand items that is a million operations. Exponential and factorial growth, O(2 to the n) and O(n factorial), become intractable past very small inputs.

A worked contrast makes the stakes concrete. With one million items, a linear algorithm performs roughly a million steps, finishing in a small fraction of a second. A quadratic one performs roughly a million million, a factor of a million more, which turns milliseconds into days on the same machine. No hardware upgrade closes a gap of that size; choosing a better algorithm is the only move that works.

Three refinements matter in practice. Best, average, and worst cases can differ sharply, and quicksort is the standard cautionary example: it averages O(n log n) but degrades to O(n squared) on already-sorted input under a naive pivot choice. Space complexity is analysed separately and by the same notation, since an algorithm that is fast but needs a copy of the data may not fit in memory. Amortized analysis handles the case where most operations are cheap and a rare one is expensive, as when a dynamic array occasionally doubles its capacity, giving an amortized O(1) append. The honest caveat is that asymptotics hide constants, so for small n a quadratic algorithm often wins outright, which is why production sorting libraries switch to insertion sort below a threshold of a few dozen elements.

sections.heading: The Four Building Blocks of Control Flow
sections.body:
Almost every algorithm ever written is assembled from a small number of control structures, and the surprising fact, proved by Corrado Bohm and Giuseppe Jacopini in 1966, is that three of them suffice. Their structured program theorem showed that sequence, selection, and iteration alone can express any computable procedure, which is the theoretical justification for abandoning unrestricted jumps and writing structured code instead. Recursion is added here as a fourth because, although it can always be rewritten as iteration, it is how a great many algorithms are most naturally expressed.

Sequence is the simplest: statements executed one after another in written order, each completing before the next begins. It sounds too obvious to name until you meet code where order has been assumed rather than enforced, and a value is read before it has been assigned.

Selection, also called branching, chooses among alternative paths according to a condition. In most languages this is an if statement, optionally chained through else-if clauses to an else that catches everything remaining, or a switch or match statement when comparing one value against many constants. Two subtleties cause real bugs. The first is that conditions are evaluated in order, so an earlier, broader condition can silently shadow a later, more specific one. The second is short-circuit evaluation: in an expression combining two tests with a logical and, most languages skip the second test entirely if the first is false. This is usually what you want, since it lets you check that a list is non-empty before reading its first element in the same expression, but it means the second test may never run and must not be relied upon for side effects.

Iteration repeats a block of steps. A while loop repeats as long as a condition holds and is right when the number of repetitions is not known in advance; a for loop repeats a fixed number of times or over each element of a collection. Every loop needs a variant, meaning some quantity that changes on each pass and guarantees the exit condition will eventually be met. Forgetting to update the loop variable, or updating it in a way that overshoots the exit test, produces an infinite loop that consumes the processor without progressing. Break exits a loop early and continue skips to the next iteration; both are useful and both make the loop's termination argument harder to see at a glance.

Recursion is a function that calls itself on a smaller instance of the same problem, with a base case that returns directly without recursing. Factorial is the canonical illustration: the factorial of n is n multiplied by the factorial of n minus one, with the factorial of zero defined as one. Recursion suits problems that are self-similar by nature, such as walking a tree or dividing and conquering, but every pending call occupies memory, so depth is bounded in a way that a loop's iteration count is not.

sections.heading: Worked Example: Linear Search vs Binary Search
sections.body:
Take a concrete task: determine whether the number 37 appears in a sorted list of sixteen numbers. Linear search examines each element from left to right until it finds a match or reaches the end. It requires no preparation, works on any list in any order, and costs up to sixteen comparisons here, or up to n comparisons in general, making it O(n). Binary search exploits the fact that the list is sorted and repeatedly discards half the remaining candidates, costing at most four comparisons here because two raised to the fourth power is sixteen, and O(log n) in general.

The procedure keeps two markers, low and high, which bracket the region where the target could still be hiding. Set low to 0 and high to 15. Compute the midpoint as low plus high divided by two using integer division, giving 7, and compare the element at index 7 with 37. If that element is smaller than 37, then 37, if present at all, must lie to the right, so set low to mid plus one, which is 8. If it is larger, the target must lie to the left, so set high to mid minus one. If it is equal, the search is finished. Repeat with the narrowed range until either a match is found or low exceeds high, at which point the target is definitively absent. The loop invariant that makes this correct is precise and worth stating: if the target is in the list at all, its index lies between low and high inclusive. Every step preserves that property while shrinking the range, so when the range becomes empty the target cannot be present.

The scale of the advantage is easy to underestimate. On a list of one million items, linear search may need a million comparisons while binary search needs at most twenty. On a billion items, binary search needs thirty. Each doubling of the data adds exactly one comparison.

Two caveats deserve emphasis. Binary search absolutely requires sorted input; run it on unsorted data and it will confidently return wrong answers rather than failing loudly, which makes it a nasty source of silent bugs. Sorting first costs O(n log n), so binary search pays for itself only when the same list will be searched many times. For a single lookup on unsorted data, one linear pass is cheaper than sorting.

Two implementation bugs are so common they are worth naming. Computing the midpoint as low plus high divided by two can overflow a fixed-width integer when both values are large; the standard fix is low plus the quantity high minus low, divided by two. This is not a theoretical concern, as a version of exactly this bug sat undetected in a widely used Java library routine for nine years. The second is mishandling the update of low and high, which typically causes either an infinite loop when the range stops shrinking or a missed element at a boundary.

sections.heading: Worked Example: Bubble Sort vs Merge Sort
sections.body:
Sorting is the most instructive comparison in the whole subject, because the same task admits algorithms whose costs differ by a factor of tens of thousands on realistic data. Bubble sort is the simplest. Walk the list from left to right, comparing each adjacent pair and swapping them whenever they are out of order. After one complete pass the largest element has been carried to the far end, hence the name, and repeating the pass on the shortened remainder eventually sorts everything. Sorting the list 5, 1, 4, 2 ascending goes like this: the first pass compares 5 with 1 and swaps to give 1, 5, 4, 2, then compares 5 with 4 and swaps to give 1, 4, 5, 2, then compares 5 with 2 and swaps to give 1, 4, 2, 5. The second pass produces 1, 2, 4, 5. Bubble sort performs up to n times n minus one, all divided by two, comparisons, which for a thousand items is about five hundred thousand, making it O(n squared). Adding a flag that records whether any swap occurred during a pass, and stopping when none did, gives it a best case of O(n) on already-sorted input, which is its one redeeming feature.

Merge sort takes the divide-and-conquer route. Split the list in half, sort each half by the same method, and then merge the two sorted halves by repeatedly taking whichever front element is smaller. The recursion bottoms out at single-element lists, which are trivially sorted. Merging the sorted pieces 1, 4 and 2, 5 compares 1 against 2 and takes 1, compares 4 against 2 and takes 2, compares 4 against 5 and takes 4, then takes the remaining 5, yielding 1, 2, 4, 5. The cost analysis is clean: halving repeatedly produces about log base two of n levels of recursion, and each level performs a total of n comparisons across all the merges at that level, so the work is n log n. That bound holds in the best, average, and worst cases alike, which is a genuine guarantee rather than an average.

Merge sort is also stable, meaning that elements comparing equal keep their original relative order. This matters more than it sounds: sorting employee records by department after already sorting them by surname leaves each department alphabetized only if the second sort is stable. The price is memory, since merging needs a buffer, giving O(n) extra space where bubble sort needs almost none.

For a million items, the quadratic method faces roughly ten to the twelve operations while the linearithmic one faces about twenty million, a ratio near fifty thousand to one. Real libraries use hybrids for exactly these reasons: Python and Java use Timsort, a merge sort adapted to exploit runs already in order, and C++ implementations typically use introsort, a quicksort that falls back to heapsort when recursion runs too deep.

sections.heading: Data Structures: Choosing How to Store Information
sections.body:
An algorithm and the structure holding its data are chosen together, because the right structure makes an algorithm short and fast while the wrong one makes the same idea slow and awkward. The single most useful habit is to ask which operation the algorithm performs most often, then pick the structure that makes that operation cheap.

An array is a contiguous block of memory holding elements of uniform size. Because the address of element k is computable directly from the start address, access by index is O(1). Insertion or deletion in the middle is O(n) because everything after the insertion point must shift. Arrays also enjoy an advantage the notation does not capture: contiguous memory is loaded into processor cache in blocks, so sequential traversal is dramatically faster than the operation count alone suggests. A linked list stores each element in a node carrying a pointer to the next, which makes insertion and deletion at a known position O(1) with no shifting, but reaching the k-th element requires following k pointers, giving O(n) access. The honest caveat is that linked lists frequently lose in practice to arrays even where the notation favours them, because each pointer hop is a potential cache miss.

A stack is a last-in, first-out container: elements are pushed and popped at one end only. It models undo history, the evaluation of nested expressions, and the call stack itself. A queue is first-in, first-out, added at the back and removed at the front, and models task scheduling, print buffers, and breadth-first traversal of a graph.

A hash table, variously called a map, dictionary, or associative array, stores key-and-value pairs. A hash function converts the key into an integer that selects a storage slot, so lookup, insertion, and deletion all average O(1) regardless of how many entries are stored, which is why hash tables underpin most fast lookup in real software. Two keys can hash to the same slot, a collision, resolved either by chaining entries in a list at that slot or by probing for a nearby free slot. Performance degrades as the load factor, the ratio of entries to slots, rises, so implementations resize and rehash at a threshold, and the worst case is O(n) if every key collides.

A tree is a hierarchy of nodes descending from a root. A binary search tree keeps smaller keys left and larger keys right, giving O(log n) search, insertion, and deletion provided it stays balanced; self-balancing variants such as red-black and AVL trees enforce that balance by rotation, since an unbalanced tree degenerates into a linked list. B-trees, with high branching factors, are the standard structure for database indexes and file systems because they minimize disk reads. A graph is a set of vertices joined by edges, modelling road networks, social connections, and dependencies, and is explored with breadth-first or depth-first search.

sections.heading: A Repeatable Problem-Solving Method
sections.body:
Thinking like a programmer is a learnable process rather than an innate gift, and the process is essentially the one the mathematician George Polya set out in 1945 for solving mathematical problems: understand the problem, devise a plan, carry out the plan, and look back. Rendered as a working loop for writing code, it becomes five steps that repay the discipline of following them in order.

Understand first. Restate the problem in your own words without using the phrasing you were given, then list the inputs, the required outputs, and the constraints, including the largest input size the solution must handle and the time available. Write two or three concrete examples by hand with their expected answers, and deliberately include the awkward ones: an empty input, a single element, all elements identical, negative numbers, the maximum permitted size. Half of all specification misunderstandings surface at this step, when they cost minutes rather than days.

Decompose next. Break the problem into sub-problems you already know how to solve, and name each one. A requirement to find whether any two numbers in a list sum to a target decomposes into sorting plus a two-pointer scan, or into a single pass plus a hash table, and either decomposition is easier to reason about than the original phrasing.

Plan in pseudocode. Write the logic in plain structured English, with the loops and branches shown but no language syntax, because this separates the thinking from the typing. Pseudocode is also the artefact you can check line by line against your hand-worked examples before a single character of real code exists, and correcting a plan is far cheaper than correcting an implementation.

Implement incrementally. Translate the pseudocode a piece at a time and run the program after each piece, rather than writing two hundred lines and then discovering that something in the middle is wrong. Keep functions small and single-purpose so that each can be tested in isolation.

Test and debug scientifically. Run the hand-made examples first, then the edge cases, then, where the input space is large, random inputs checked against a slow but obviously correct reference implementation. When something fails, resist changing code at random. Form a specific hypothesis about what is wrong, devise an observation that would confirm or refute it, insert a print statement or set a breakpoint that makes the relevant variable visible at the relevant moment, and then look. If the failing region is large, bisect it: check a value halfway through the computation to determine which half contains the fault, and repeat. This is binary search applied to your own program and it converges fast. Explaining the code aloud, line by line, to a colleague or an inanimate object, the practice known as rubber-duck debugging, works far more often than it has any right to, because articulating each step forces you to state assumptions you had been silently making.

sections.heading: Common Mistakes and Pitfalls
sections.body:
A small number of mistakes account for a large share of the bugs beginners write, and knowing their shapes in advance is the cheapest debugging technique available.

Off-by-one errors head the list. They arise from confusing a strict less-than with a less-than-or-equal in a loop condition, or from mishandling zero-based indexing, where the first element of a list of length n sits at index 0 and the last at index n minus one. A loop written to run up to and including index n reads one element past the end, which in a memory-safe language raises an error and in an unsafe one silently reads whatever happens to be adjacent. Infinite loops are the close relation: the loop variable is never updated, or is updated in a way that skips over the exit condition entirely, as when a counter increments by two but the test checks for exact equality with an odd number.

Ignoring edge cases produces code that handles the typical input and fails on the boundaries. Always ask what happens with an empty collection, a single element, duplicate values, and the maximum permitted size, and check those cases explicitly rather than assuming they behave like the middle of the range.

Numeric assumptions bite hard. Integers in most languages have a fixed width, and a 32-bit signed integer overflows above 2,147,483,647, wrapping silently to a large negative number; a unit-conversion overflow of exactly this kind destroyed the Ariane 5 rocket on its first flight in 1996. Integer division truncates, so seven divided by two yields three rather than three and a half in most languages, and the remainder is silently discarded. Floating-point arithmetic is not exact in decimal terms, so adding 0.1 to 0.2 does not produce exactly 0.3, and floating-point values should be compared with a small tolerance rather than tested for equality.

Unchecked assumptions form their own category: running binary search on unsorted data, trusting that input is well-formed without validating it, or modifying a collection while iterating over it, which many languages either forbid outright or permit with undefined and surprising results.

Premature optimization deserves its own warning. Donald Knuth's much-quoted remark, that premature optimization is the root of all evil, is usually cited without its qualifier, which is that programmers should forget about small efficiencies about ninety-seven percent of the time. The working order is to make it correct, make it clear, then measure with realistic data, then optimize only the part the measurement identifies as the bottleneck. Intuition about where time is spent is famously unreliable.

Finally, duplicating logic by copy and paste multiplies every future bug by the number of copies, since a fix applied to one copy leaves the others broken. Write a function once, name variables so their meaning is obvious without a comment, test as you go, and argue about correctness for all inputs rather than trusting a single passing example.

sections.heading: Greedy Algorithms and Dynamic Programming: Two Higher-Level Strategies
sections.body:
Growth notation tells you how an algorithm scales but says nothing about which strategy to reach for when designing one. Two general strategies sit above individual algorithms such as sorting and searching, and recognizing which one a problem admits is a large part of algorithmic skill.

A greedy algorithm builds a solution one step at a time, always taking whichever choice looks best at that moment, and never reconsidering. Making change illustrates it well. With United States coin denominations of 1, 5, 10 and 25 cents, repeatedly grabbing the largest coin that does not overshoot always produces the fewest coins possible: 41 cents becomes 25 plus 10 plus 5 plus 1, four coins, which is genuinely optimal. But greedy is not universally safe. Invent a currency with denominations 1, 3 and 4 and ask for 6 cents. Greedy takes a 4 first, leaving 2, which it can only make as 1 plus 1, for three coins in total, while the true optimum is two coins, 3 plus 3. The greedy approach failed because that denomination set lacks the property, present in the US set, that a locally best choice never forecloses a globally better solution. The general lesson is that greedy algorithms are fast, typically O(n log n) or better since each candidate is considered once, but they require a proof rather than an intuition. Dijkstra's shortest-path algorithm, Huffman coding for data compression, and the activity-selection problem of scheduling the most non-overlapping meetings are all greedy and all provably correct; the standard proof technique is an exchange argument, showing that any optimal solution can be transformed step by step into the greedy one without getting worse.

Dynamic programming is what you reach for when greedy cannot be justified but the problem has two properties: optimal substructure, meaning an optimal solution is built from optimal solutions to sub-problems, and overlapping sub-problems, meaning a naive recursive solution solves the same smaller instance many times over. Fibonacci numbers are the textbook demonstration. Defining fib of n as fib of n minus one plus fib of n minus two and computing it recursively recomputes the same values inside both branches, and the number of calls grows roughly as two to the n, so fib of 40 alone triggers well over a billion redundant calls. Storing each result the first time it is computed and reusing it thereafter, a technique called memoization, collapses the running time from exponential to linear.

The same trick has two standard shapes. Top-down memoization keeps the recursive structure and adds a cache. Bottom-up tabulation fills a table from the smallest sub-problems upward and avoids recursion entirely, which is usually faster and never risks exhausting the stack. Applied to two dimensions, it solves the zero-one knapsack problem of choosing items to maximize value within a weight limit, edit distance for spelling suggestions, and the Needleman-Wunsch algorithm of 1970 for aligning DNA sequences. The honest caveat is that dynamic programming trades memory for time, and knapsack's table of size n times W is only pseudo-polynomial, since W is a numeric value rather than an input length.

sections.heading: Recursion, the Call Stack, and When It Breaks
sections.body:
Recursion is often introduced as a stylistic alternative to a loop, but treating it that way hides a real mechanical cost that eventually shows up as a crash. Every function call, recursive or not, pushes a stack frame onto the call stack: a block of memory holding that call's parameters, its local variables, and the return address it must jump back to when it finishes. A recursive call does not somehow reuse the frame of the call that made it. It pushes a fresh one, even though it is nominally the same function, and that frame persists until the call returns.

Trace the factorial of 5 by hand to see the shape of it. Calling factorial with 5 pushes a frame and, before it can compute anything, calls factorial with 4, which pushes its own frame and calls factorial with 3, and so on down to factorial with 0, the base case, which returns 1 immediately without recursing. At that instant five frames sit in memory simultaneously, each mid-execution, each suspended waiting on the call beneath it. Only when the base case returns does the call for 1 resume, multiply 1 by 1, and return 1 to the call for 2, which returns 2, then 6, then 24, and finally 120. The stack grew to depth five and unwound to zero. An iterative loop keeping a single running total would have used one frame throughout, and this difference is the entire cost of recursion.

The consequence is hard rather than gradual. Recursion that goes too deep exhausts the stack and crashes with a stack overflow. On a typical system the main thread's stack is a few megabytes and a worker thread's is often one megabyte, which at perhaps 50 to 100 bytes of frame overhead per call permits tens of thousands of levels, not millions. Python imposes an explicit recursion limit, 1,000 nested calls by default, precisely so that what would otherwise be an unrecoverable memory fault becomes a catchable exception; raising that limit with sys.setrecursionlimit does not enlarge the underlying stack and simply moves the failure from a clean exception to a genuine crash. The commonest way beginners trigger the problem is a missing base case, or a base case that exists but is never reached because the recursive step does not reliably move toward it, for instance recursing on n minus one when n can be negative.

Some languages optimize tail recursion, the special case where the recursive call is the last thing the function does with no pending work afterward, by reusing the current frame rather than pushing a new one, which turns the recursion into a loop at the machine level. This is not universal. Python deliberately declines to implement it, on the stated reasoning that stack traces should remain honest and complete. When depth must genuinely scale with the input, as when traversing a very deep tree, the standard remedy is to rewrite the algorithm iteratively with an explicit stack structure you manage on the heap, which has no comparable fixed limit.

sections.heading: Equipment You'll Actually Need
sections.body:
This is among the cheapest subjects in the whole collection to practise seriously, because the only genuinely irreplaceable resources are time and attention. A second-hand computer a decade old will execute a million operations in a small fraction of a second, which is more than enough to make every timing difference described here plainly visible, and nothing on the list below costs money that a public library cannot cover.

A few of the choices deserve a word of justification. A plain text editor is genuinely sufficient to start, and there is an argument for beginning with one, since a full development environment corrects typing mistakes so helpfully that a learner never builds the habit of reading their own code carefully. Python is recommended not because it is fastest, which it is not, but because its syntax carries so little ceremony that the algorithm remains legible on the page, and because it ships already installed on most systems that are not running Windows.

Paper matters more than it looks. Tracing an algorithm by hand, writing out the value of every variable after every iteration in a small table, is the fastest way to discover that your mental model of a loop and the loop's actual behaviour differ. It is also the only reliable way to check a plan before committing to code.

For timing, prefer the language's own high-resolution timer over a stopwatch. A wall-clock timer typically resolves to around fifteen milliseconds, which is far coarser than many of the runs you will want to measure, whereas a performance counter resolves to microseconds or better. Run each measurement several times and take the shortest result rather than the average, because background activity on the machine can only ever make a run slower, never faster.

The playing cards and index cards are not decoration. Physically sorting a spread hand using only adjacent swaps, then again by splitting and merging, converts an abstract cost difference into something your hands have felt, and it is remarkably effective at making the distinction stick.
ingredients: A computer with a free code editor or even a plain text editor installed
A free programming language interpreter — Python is the most common starting choice for algorithm practice and is freely downloadable, or already installed, on most systems
Pen and paper, or a whiteboard, for tracing an algorithm's execution step by step by hand before trusting it to a computer
A stopwatch, or simply the timing functions built into your chosen language, for measuring real runtime differences between algorithms

A deck of playing cards, genuinely useful for physically practicing sorting algorithms (spread a shuffled hand face-up and sort it using only bubble-sort-style adjacent swaps, then again by merge-sort-style splitting)
A stack of index cards or sticky notes, handy for modeling a call stack or a stack/queue data structure by hand

sections.heading: Step-by-Step: Trace and Time Three Sorting Algorithms Yourself
sections.body:
Reading that one growth rate beats another is easy to accept and easy to forget. Watching the gap open up on your own machine, in numbers you measured yourself, is what makes it permanent, and the exercise below is designed so that the arithmetic of the result is checkable in advance rather than merely observed.

The prediction to test is precise. Quadratic cost means that multiplying the input size by four should multiply the running time by roughly sixteen, because four squared is sixteen. Linearithmic cost means the same fourfold increase should multiply the time by only a little more than four: the n factor contributes exactly four, and the log n factor contributes the ratio of the logarithms, which for five thousand rising to twenty thousand is about 14.3 divided by 12.3, or 1.16, giving roughly 4.6 in total. Those two predicted ratios, sixteen against about four and a half, are the whole point of the measurement.

Two practical warnings before starting. A bubble sort of twenty thousand elements in an interpreted language performs about two hundred million comparisons and can take a minute or more, so start with the smaller size and scale up rather than launching the largest run first. And run each timing at least three times, keeping the fastest, since other activity on the machine adds noise that only ever slows a run down. Use the same generated list for both algorithms in a given trial so that the comparison is fair.
steps: Write (or find and understand line-by-line) a working bubble sort function and a working merge sort function in your chosen language.

Pick 10 random two-digit numbers, write them on paper, and trace bubble sort by hand: repeatedly scan left to right swapping any adjacent out-of-order pair, and count exactly how many comparisons and swaps the full sort takes.
Trace merge sort by hand on the same 10 numbers: recursively split the list in half until each piece has one element, then merge pairs back together in sorted order, again counting comparisons.
Compare the two counts — bubble sort should take noticeably more comparisons even on this tiny list, and the gap only widens as the list grows.

Generate a random list of 5,000 numbers in code (most languages have a built-in random module) and time how long your bubble sort and merge sort each take, using the language's timing functions; record both numbers.
Repeat with 20,000 numbers (four times the size) and record the new times.
Compare the ratios: bubble sort's time should have grown roughly 16x (quadratically, matching O(n squared)) while merge sort's time grew only a bit more than 4x (matching O(n log n)).

Finally, time both algorithms on an already-sorted list of 20,000 numbers and then a reverse-sorted one, and notice bubble sort (with an early-exit flag added) finishes almost instantly on the sorted case but merge sort's time barely changes — a direct, hands-on demonstration of best-case versus worst-case behavior.

guides.title: Encoding, Data & Compression
guides.summary: How numbers, text, images and sound are all reduced to bits; Shannon's measure of information; how lossless and lossy compression shrink data; and how parity, checksums and error-correcting codes detect and repair the inevitable bit errors.

sections.heading: Representing Numbers: Integers, Negatives and Floats
sections.body: Everything inside a computer is a pattern of bits, and a bit pattern carries no meaning on its own. The meaning comes entirely from the encoding both sides have agreed to use, which is why the same 32 bits can be an integer, a colour, four letters or a fragment of sound depending only on what the reading code expects. Unsigned integers use plain binary, so eight bits cover 0 to 255, sixteen bits cover 0 to 65,535, and thirty-two bits cover 0 to about 4.29 billion. Negative numbers use a scheme called two's complement, in which the leftmost bit indicates sign and a negative value is formed by inverting every bit of its magnitude and then adding one. In eight-bit two's complement, positive five is 00000101; to get negative five you invert to 11111010 and add one to reach 11111011. The reason for this apparently convoluted arrangement is elegant and practical: it lets one adder circuit perform both addition and subtraction, since subtracting a number is identical to adding its two's complement, and it gives exactly one representation of zero rather than the separate positive and negative zeroes that simpler sign-and-magnitude schemes produce. The range is asymmetric, from negative 128 to positive 127, because the pattern that would be negative zero is reused for the extra negative value. That asymmetry causes a real bug: negating the most negative integer overflows silently, since positive 128 does not exist in eight bits. Fractional numbers use floating point, standardised as IEEE 754 and implemented in essentially every processor. A thirty-two-bit single-precision float divides into one sign bit, eight exponent bits and twenty-three fraction or mantissa bits, and represents a value of plus or minus one-point-fraction multiplied by two raised to the exponent minus 127. This is scientific notation in base two, and it buys enormous range, roughly ten to the minus thirty-eight through ten to the thirty-eight, at the cost of limited precision: about seven decimal digits for single precision, about fifteen or sixteen for the sixty-four-bit double. The consequence trips up every programmer eventually. Adding 0.1 and 0.2 does not produce exactly 0.3, because one tenth has no exact finite binary expansion, exactly as one third has no exact finite decimal expansion. The stored value is the nearest representable number, and the tiny errors accumulate. The working rule is never to test floating-point values for exact equality; compare the absolute difference against a small tolerance, conventionally called epsilon, chosen to suit the magnitudes involved. For money, avoid binary floats altogether and use integer counts of the smallest unit, such as whole cents, or a decimal type. IEEE 754 also reserves patterns for special values that every programmer eventually meets: positive and negative infinity, produced by overflow or division by zero, and not-a-number, produced by operations such as zero divided by zero or the square root of a negative. Not-a-number has the disconcerting property of comparing unequal to everything including itself, which is the standard trick for detecting it. The format also carries a negative zero distinct from positive zero, though the two compare as equal.

sections.heading: Representing Text: ASCII, Unicode and UTF-8
sections.body: Text is stored by mapping each character to a number, called a code point, and then storing that number's bits. The first widely adopted mapping, ASCII, was standardised in 1963 and uses seven bits to cover 128 values: the unaccented English letters, the digits, common punctuation and thirty-three non-printing control codes inherited from teleprinters. Capital A is 65, lowercase a is 97, the digit zero is 48 and space is 32. Two details of that layout are deliberate and still exploited constantly. The letters are contiguous, so subtracting the code of A from the code of C gives two, which is how alphabetical arithmetic and range checks work. The gap between uppercase and lowercase is exactly 32, a single bit, so changing case is a one-bit operation. ASCII cannot express accented letters, non-Latin scripts, mathematical symbols or emoji, and the patchwork of incompatible eight-bit extensions that filled the gap through the 1980s and 1990s created endless corruption. Unicode replaced them by assigning a unique code point to every character in every writing system, now more than 149,000 of them, written as U plus four or more hexadecimal digits. U+00E9 is the letter e with an acute accent, U+4E2D is the Chinese character for middle, and U+1F600 is a grinning face. Unicode defines the numbers; it does not by itself say how to store them as bytes, and that is a separate decision called an encoding. UTF-8 is the dominant answer and now covers the overwhelming majority of web content. It is variable-width: one byte for the original ASCII range, two bytes for most European and Middle Eastern scripts, three for most Asian scripts, and four for emoji and rarer symbols. Two properties explain its victory. First, any valid ASCII file is already valid UTF-8 with identical bytes, so decades of existing data and software kept working. Second, it is self-synchronising: the leading byte of a multi-byte sequence has a distinctive bit pattern and continuation bytes have another, so a decoder that starts mid-stream, or that hits corruption, can find the next character boundary without scanning from the beginning. The classic failure mode is mojibake, garbled text produced when bytes written in one encoding are read as another, so that a UTF-8 accented character decoded as Latin-1 appears as two nonsense symbols. The remedy is discipline rather than cleverness: store and transmit the encoding explicitly, default to UTF-8 everywhere, and never rely on a system's locale to guess. A related trap is that a Unicode character is not always one code point, since accents can be composed separately, so counting characters correctly requires care. The letter e with an acute accent can be stored either as the single code point U+00E9 or as a plain e followed by a combining acute accent, and the two look identical on screen while comparing unequal byte for byte. Unicode defines normalisation forms to resolve this, and any system comparing user-entered text, such as usernames or filenames, should normalise first. Emoji compound the problem, since a single visible glyph such as a family or a flag can be built from several code points joined by invisible connectors.

sections.heading: Representing Images, Color and Sound
sections.body:
A digital image is a rectangular grid of picture elements, or pixels, each storing a colour as a group of numbers. The most common colour model is RGB, which gives the intensity of red, green and blue light, conventionally as three values from 0 to 255. Eight bits per channel gives twenty-four-bit true colour and 16.7 million distinct colours, comfortably more than the eye can distinguish in a single scene. Pure red is 255, 0, 0; white is 255, 255, 255; black is 0, 0, 0. The model is additive because it describes emitted light, which is why mixing red and green light yields yellow, against the subtractive intuition from mixing paint. A fourth alpha channel can be added to record transparency, giving RGBA at thirty-two bits per pixel. The storage arithmetic is worth doing once, because it explains why compression is not optional. A 1920 by 1080 image at twenty-four bits per pixel occupies 1920 times 1080 times 3 bytes, about 6.2 megabytes uncompressed; thirty such frames per second is roughly 187 megabytes per second of video.

Sound is a continuous pressure wave, and turning it into numbers requires two separate approximations. Sampling measures the wave's amplitude at regular intervals, and quantisation rounds each measurement to the nearest representable value. Compact disc audio samples 44,100 times per second at sixteen bits per sample, which yields about 1.4 million bits per second for two channels. The sample rate is not arbitrary.
