The Nyquist-Shannon sampling theorem states that to reconstruct a signal exactly you must sample at more than twice its highest frequency component; human hearing extends to roughly 20,000 hertz, so a rate above 40,000 is required, and 44,100 leaves margin for the anti-aliasing filter that removes higher frequencies before conversion. Skip that filter and frequencies above half the sample rate do not simply vanish; they fold back down and appear as spurious lower tones, an artefact called aliasing that is impossible to remove afterwards. Bit depth sets the noise floor rather than the frequency range, at roughly six decibels of dynamic range per bit, so sixteen bits gives about ninety-six decibels. Every medium follows the same underlying pattern: take a physical quantity that varies continuously, measure it at intervals, round each measurement, and store the resulting numbers as bits. Everything that follows, including all compression, operates on those numbers rather than on the original phenomenon.

Two further points about colour are worth carrying. The 0 to 255 values are usually not linear measures of light; they are gamma-encoded, meaning the scale is deliberately compressed at the bright end and stretched at the dark end to match the eye's greater sensitivity to shadow detail. This is why averaging two pixel values naively produces a result darker than the true optical average, a subtle bug in image-resizing code. Second, an RGB triple means nothing absolute without a colour space specifying what the primaries and white point physically are. The same numbers under the sRGB and Display P3 specifications produce visibly different colours, which is why images carry an embedded colour profile and why a photograph can look right in one application and oversaturated in another.

sections.heading: Information Theory: Entropy and the Limits of Compression
sections.body:
Claude Shannon's 1948 paper A Mathematical Theory of Communication supplied the mathematical foundation for all compression, and it did so by defining information as a measurable quantity rather than a vague notion. The core insight is that information is surprise. An event you already expected tells you nothing; an event you thought unlikely tells you a great deal. Formally, the information content of an event of probability p is the negative base-two logarithm of p, measured in bits. A certain event, with probability one, carries exactly zero bits, because being told it happened changes nothing. A fair coin flip, probability one half, carries one bit. An event of probability one in a thousand carries almost ten bits. Base two is chosen so that the unit is the bit; using natural logarithms would give nats and using base ten would give hartleys, and the choice affects only the scale.

Entropy, written H, is the average information per symbol emitted by a source: the sum over all symbols of each symbol's probability multiplied by its information content, measured in bits per symbol. Entropy is the theoretical floor for lossless compression. You cannot, on average, encode a source in fewer bits per symbol than its entropy, and Shannon's source coding theorem proves both that the bound holds and that it can be approached arbitrarily closely. Work an example to make it concrete. Consider a source emitting four symbols with probabilities one half, one quarter, one eighth and one eighth. Their information contents are one, two, three and three bits respectively. The entropy is therefore one half times one, plus one quarter times two, plus one eighth times three, plus one eighth times three, which sums to 1.75 bits per symbol. A naive fixed-width code would spend two bits on each of four symbols, so an ideal code saves 12.5 percent, and no code can do better without loss.

Two consequences follow that matter in practice. The first is that compression works only because real data is far from random. English text, photographs, program source and recorded sound all carry heavy structure and repetition, so their entropy per symbol is well below the naive maximum, and that gap is the redundancy a compressor removes. Printed English has been estimated at roughly one to one-and-a-half bits per letter against the naive 4.7 bits needed for twenty-six letters plus a space. The second consequence is that already-compressed or genuinely random data cannot be compressed further, and a counting argument proves that no algorithm can shrink every possible input: if it shortens some inputs it must lengthen others, because there are simply fewer short bit strings than long ones. Any tool claiming otherwise is mistaken. This is why zipping a JPEG or an encrypted archive gains almost nothing, and occasionally adds a few bytes of header.

sections.heading: Lossless Compression: RLE and Huffman Coding
sections.body:
Lossless compression shrinks data in a way that permits perfect reconstruction of the original bit-for-bit, which makes it the only acceptable choice for text, program code, archives, spreadsheets and any record whose exact content matters. Two foundational methods illustrate the whole family, and both are simple enough to perform by hand.

Run-length encoding replaces a run of identical values with a count and the value itself. The nine-character string of six A's followed by three B's becomes a four-character description meaning six A then three B, cutting the size by more than half. The method is excellent where long runs genuinely occur, as in simple line graphics, scanned fax documents and screen captures of flat-coloured interfaces, and it costs almost nothing to implement. Its weakness is equally sharp: on data without runs, every single character must still be preceded by a count of one, so the output can be nearly twice the input. Practical formats therefore either use run-length encoding on data known to suit it or combine it with other stages, and they include an escape mechanism so that incompressible stretches are stored literally.

Huffman coding, published by David Huffman in 1952 while he was a graduate student, takes a different route: instead of exploiting repetition it exploits unequal frequency, assigning short bit codes to common symbols and long codes to rare ones so that the average length falls. The construction is a bottom-up tree. List every symbol with its frequency, repeatedly take the two lowest-frequency nodes and merge them into a new node whose weight is their sum, and continue until a single tree remains. Reading from the root to each leaf, taking a left branch as zero and a right branch as one, gives that symbol's code. The construction guarantees a crucial property: no code is a prefix of any other, which makes the compressed stream decodable unambiguously without separators, since as soon as the accumulated bits match a leaf the symbol is complete. Applied to the four-symbol source with probabilities one half, one quarter, one eighth and one eighth, Huffman produces codes of length one, two, three and three, averaging exactly 1.75 bits and hitting the entropy bound precisely. That exact match happens only when every probability is a power of one half; otherwise Huffman is provably optimal among whole-bit codes but can exceed entropy by up to one bit per symbol, which is why arithmetic and range coders, which can spend fractional bits, do better on skewed alphabets. Real compressors such as DEFLATE, the engine inside ZIP, gzip and PNG, combine a dictionary stage with Huffman coding to approach the limit on ordinary data. One practical detail is easy to overlook: the decoder needs the code table, so either it must be stored in the compressed file, costing space that matters on small inputs, or both sides must agree on a fixed table in advance, which performs badly when the data does not match expectations. DEFLATE hedges by choosing per block between a stored literal block, a fixed standard table and a custom table written into the stream.

sections.heading: Dictionary Methods and Lossy Compression
sections.body:
Dictionary compression, introduced by Abraham Lempel and Jacob Ziv in 1977 and universally called LZ77, works on repetition rather than frequency. As it scans the input it keeps a sliding window of recently seen bytes, and whenever the upcoming text matches something already in that window it emits a back-reference giving the distance backwards and the length to copy. In the phrase about a cat sitting on a mat, the second occurrence of the word 'the' plus its space becomes a short pointer to the first. Because the dictionary is the data already decoded, no table needs to be transmitted, and the decoder rebuilds it as it goes. This single idea is why text, source code, log files and HTML compress so dramatically, often to a quarter or a fifth of their size, and it underlies ZIP, gzip, PNG and the successors zstd and Brotli. Window size is the main tuning knob: a larger window finds more distant repeats but costs memory and time.

Lossy compression takes a fundamentally different bargain, permanently discarding information that human perception is poor at detecting in exchange for much smaller files. JPEG divides a photograph into blocks of eight by eight pixels and applies the discrete cosine transform, re-expressing each block as a sum of spatial frequency patterns rather than as individual pixel values. It then quantises, meaning rounds coarsely, the high-frequency coefficients, because the eye is far less sensitive to fine detail than to broad changes in brightness. The quality setting controls how coarse that rounding is; push it too low and the block boundaries become visible as square artefacts. Typical photographs survive roughly ten to one compression with little visible loss. MP3 and AAC apply the same philosophy to sound through a psychoacoustic model, discarding frequencies masked by louder nearby tones, and achieve a similar ratio. Video codecs such as H.264 and H.265 add the largest saving of all by storing mainly the differences between successive frames, since most of a scene is unchanged from one frame to the next.

The governing rule is straightforward. Use lossless compression for anything that must be reproduced exactly, including text, source code, and medical, scientific, forensic or legal images, where a discarded detail could change a diagnosis or a verdict. Use lossy compression only for perceptual media where small imperfections are genuinely acceptable. Above all, never repeatedly re-save a lossy file, because each save quantises the already-quantised result and the damage accumulates, an effect called generation loss. Keep a lossless master, edit from that, and export to the lossy format once.

One boundary case causes genuine confusion. Some formats are lossy in a way that is easy to miss because no visible artefact appears. Reducing a full-colour image to a 256-entry palette, as the GIF format requires, discards colour information permanently even though the encoder itself is lossless afterwards; the loss happened at the palette step. Resizing an image down and saving it as PNG likewise produces a lossless file of irretrievably reduced data. Lossless describes the compression stage, not the whole pipeline, and it is the pipeline that determines whether the original can be recovered.

sections.heading: Error Detection and Correction
sections.body:
Storage and transmission are never perfect. Cosmic rays and background radiation flip bits in memory, electrical noise corrupts signals on a wire, scratches destroy sectors on a disc, and flash cells wear out and drift. The response is to add controlled redundancy, extra bits computed from the data, so that corruption is either caught or repaired. The whole field is a trade-off between how many extra bits you are willing to spend and how much protection you get.

The simplest scheme is a single parity bit. Append one bit chosen so that the total number of ones is even, which is called even parity. If exactly one bit flips anywhere in the protected group, the count becomes odd and the receiver knows something is wrong. The limitations are severe and worth stating plainly: it detects any odd number of errors but is blind to any even number, since two flips cancel, and even when it detects an error it cannot say which bit was wrong, so it cannot repair anything. Checksums and cyclic redundancy checks are far stronger. A CRC treats the message as the coefficients of a polynomial, divides by a fixed generator polynomial, and transmits the remainder; the receiver repeats the division and compares. CRC-32 is used in Ethernet frames, ZIP archives and disk sectors precisely because polynomial division is excellent at catching burst errors, the clustered runs of corruption that physical media actually produce, and it is cheap in hardware. A CRC still only detects. It is also not a security measure, because an attacker who alters the data can simply recompute the CRC; that job belongs to cryptographic hashes.

Hamming codes, devised by Richard Hamming in 1950 out of frustration with a relay computer that halted every time it found an error, go further and repair. Parity bits are placed at power-of-two positions, each covering a different overlapping subset of the data bits, so that when the receiver recomputes them the pattern of failures spells out, in binary, the position of the faulty bit. Flipping that bit back restores the message. A seven-four Hamming code protects four data bits with three parity bits and corrects any single-bit error; adding one more overall parity bit lets it also detect, though not correct, any double error. Error-correcting-code memory and RAID storage arrays extend the same principles so that servers survive routine bit flips and disk failures without human intervention.

Work a check by hand. To send the four bits one, zero, one, one under even parity, count the ones: there are three, an odd number, so the parity bit must be one, and the transmitted group is one, zero, one, one, one. If the receiver sees one, zero, one, zero, one it counts three ones, an odd total where an even one was promised, and rejects the group. The engineering judgement is always the same: match the strength of the code to how noisy the channel actually is, since redundancy you do not need is pure cost.

sections.heading: Real-World Formats: How ZIP, PNG, JPEG and MP3 Combine These Ideas
sections.body:
Nobody ships raw entropy calculations or a bare Huffman tree as a finished product. Real file formats stack several distinct techniques on top of one another, and knowing the stack explains a great deal of everyday computing behaviour that otherwise looks arbitrary.

Take PNG, a lossless image format. Before compressing anything, PNG runs a filter pass over each row of pixels, replacing each pixel's stored value with the difference from a predicted value, often just the pixel to its left or an average of its neighbours. Because photographs and screenshots are mostly smooth, the great majority of these differences cluster near zero, which is exactly the low-entropy, repetitive data that compresses well. The filter is chosen per row, so a single image can mix strategies. Only after this prediction step does PNG hand the result to DEFLATE, the same general-purpose algorithm used inside ZIP, which combines LZ77-style dictionary matching with Huffman coding on whatever remains. This layering is why zipping an already-compressed JPEG barely shrinks it: DEFLATE is hunting for redundancy the JPEG encoder already removed.

JPEG itself takes the lossy route. It splits an image into blocks of eight by eight pixels and applies the discrete cosine transform to each, re-expressing the block's pixel values as a sum of cosine wave patterns of increasing spatial frequency. It then quantises the high-frequency coefficients much more aggressively than the low-frequency ones, because human vision is far less sensitive to fine detail than to broad shifts in brightness and colour. That quantisation is the actual lossy step, and it is tunable, which is what the quality slider in an image editor controls. Most JPEG encoders also subsample the colour channels relative to brightness, typically storing colour at half resolution, for the same perceptual reason. Whatever coefficients survive are then run-length and Huffman coded, the same lossless finishing move PNG uses. Because information is permanently discarded at quantisation, repeatedly opening, editing and re-saving a JPEG accumulates fresh rounding loss each time, which is why professional workflows edit from an uncompressed or losslessly compressed master and export to JPEG once, at the end. Rotating by exact multiples of ninety degrees is the notable exception, since good tools can do it without re-encoding the blocks.

MP3 applies the same lossy philosophy to sound using a psychoacoustic model instead of a visual one. It exploits auditory masking, the well-documented fact that a loud tone renders nearby quieter frequencies, and sounds immediately following it, inaudible even though they remain physically present in the waveform. The encoder discards those masked components before Huffman-coding what is left, which is how a 128 kilobit-per-second MP3 squeezes compact-disc audio of roughly 1,411 kilobits per second down to about one-eleventh of its size while still sounding close to the original to most listeners on most equipment.

sections.heading: Base64 and the Practical Problem of Moving Binary Data as Text
sections.body:
Every encoding scheme so far assumes the receiving system can carry arbitrary binary bytes. In practice, large parts of the infrastructure the internet is built on, including early email transport, URLs, JSON documents and XML, were designed to carry printable text only, and they choke on or silently mangle raw byte values below 32 or above 126. Some mail gateways historically stripped the eighth bit outright, and several byte values still function as control characters in transport protocols. Base64 exists to move arbitrary binary data through these text-only pipes intact.

The mechanism is a change of base. Binary data is naturally grouped in eight-bit bytes, whereas Base64 regroups the identical bit stream into six-bit chunks, because two to the sixth is 64 and 64 characters is exactly enough to cover the twenty-six uppercase letters, twenty-six lowercase letters, ten digits and two extra symbols, conventionally plus and slash, all of which are safely printable ASCII. Since eight and six share no common multiple below twenty-four, the encoder processes three input bytes at a time, which is twenty-four bits, and re-slices that block into four six-bit groups. Three bytes in, four printable characters out.

Walk it through by hand on the word Cat. The three ASCII bytes are 67, 97 and 116, which in binary are 01000011, 01100001 and 01110100. Concatenated into one twenty-four-bit stream and re-cut into four six-bit groups they read 010000, 110110, 000101, 110100, which in decimal are 16, 54, 5 and 52. Looking each index up in the Base64 alphabet, where A is 0 through Z at 25, a is 26 through z at 51, the digit zero is 52 through nine at 61, and plus and slash are 62 and 63, gives the characters Q, 2, F and 0. So Cat encodes to the four-character string Q2F0. Notice the output is four characters for three input bytes, so Base64 inflates data by exactly one third, a real and frequently forgotten cost in storage and bandwidth. When the input length is not a clean multiple of three, the encoder pads the final group with one or two equals signs so the decoder knows how many trailing bits to discard.

It is worth being blunt about what Base64 is not. It is neither encryption nor compression: it adds no secrecy whatsoever, since anyone can decode it instantly and many tools do so automatically, and it makes data larger rather than smaller. Its entire job is compatibility. That is why images embedded directly in a web page's HTML or CSS appear as a long data URI, why email attachments travel as blocks of Base64 text underneath, and why the first two segments of a JSON Web Token carrying login session data are readable Base64 rather than raw bytes. In every case the payload has been re-based purely so it survives a text-only channel. A URL-safe variant substitutes minus and underscore for plus and slash, because those two characters have reserved meanings inside a URL.

sections.heading: Equipment You'll Actually Need
sections.body: Most of the practical work in this subject needs only software you almost certainly already have, and the few physical props involved are cheap and serve a specific pedagogical purpose rather than being decoration. It is worth understanding why each item earns its place. A hex editor, or the hex-dump command built into essentially every operating system, matters more than anything else on the list, because encoding is invisible until you look at raw bytes. Opening a small text file in hex and seeing the exact ASCII codes, then saving the same text with an accented character and watching a single visible letter occupy two bytes, converts UTF-8 from an abstraction into something observed. A scripting language interpreter with built-in compression, Base64 and bit manipulation lets you check every hand calculation in seconds, which is the difference between believing a result and verifying it; use it to confirm answers you have already worked out rather than to produce them. A calculator with a programmer or binary mode removes the tedium from base conversion once you have done enough conversions by hand to understand what it is doing. An image editor able to export the same picture as an uncompressed bitmap, a PNG and a JPEG gives the single most persuasive demonstration in the whole subject, because the three file sizes side by side make the lossless and lossy trade-offs concrete in a way no explanation matches. Playing cards or dice are included for a subtle reason: hand-generated random data is the control case. Compressing a page of repeated text and then compressing an equally long string of dice rolls demonstrates directly that compression exploits structure and that genuinely random data will not shrink, which is the practical face of the entropy bound. A Unix-like terminal is optional but convenient, since the standard archive utilities report ratios directly and byte-inspection tools compose into one-line experiments. The honest caveat about all of it is that file sizes reported by a graphical file browser include format headers and are rounded to allocation blocks, so small test files can give misleading ratios.
ingredients: A computer with a plain text editor and, ideally, a free hex editor (or a terminal capable of a hex dump, which most operating systems include by default) for inspecting raw bytes directly
A free scripting language interpreter such as Python, which has built-in support for compression (gzip/zlib), Base64 and bit-level manipulation without installing anything extra
A calculator with a 'programmer' or binary/hex conversion mode (a free feature on most phone and desktop calculator apps), or paper for manual binary math
A basic image-editing program capable of exporting the same picture as BMP, PNG and JPEG (many free/built-in ones can), for direct side-by-side file-size comparison
A pack of playing cards or a pair of dice, useful for hand-generating genuinely random data to compare against structured, repetitive data when testing how well something compresses
Optional: a Unix-like terminal (built into Linux and macOS; addable on Windows) for using standard zip/gzip utilities and byte-inspection tools directly on real files

sections.heading: Step-by-Step: Encode, Compress and Measure Data by Hand
sections.body: The fastest way to genuinely trust that Huffman coding and Base64 work is to push a short piece of data through each of them by hand and check the arithmetic yourself. Two aspects deserve explanation, being where the real learning sits. The first is the comparison between the hand calculation and what a real archive utility reports. A hand-built Huffman code for a short string shows a substantial percentage saving, and the zip file of the same string shows almost none, or may even be larger than the original. That is not an arithmetic mistake. Every archive format carries fixed overhead: a local file header, a central directory entry, the filename, timestamps and a CRC, together running to roughly a hundred bytes regardless of content. On a file of a dozen bytes that overhead dominates, and the lesson generalises to real systems, where compressing many tiny files individually is worse than archiving them together first. The second aspect is the visual inspection of the JPEG. Zooming hard into a sharp, high-contrast edge and looking for faint square patterning shows the eight-by-eight block grid the transform operates on, the only point in the subject where a lossy algorithm's internal structure becomes visible to the naked eye. Choose an image with a hard boundary, such as text on a plain background, and save it at low quality; a soft photograph hides it. Work the sequence with a pen rather than in your head, because the tree construction has a tie-breaking choice at each merge, and writing it down is what makes the code table reproducible.
steps: Take the string 'ABRACADABRA' (11 characters) and count each letter's frequency: A=5, B=2, R=2, C=1, D=1.

Build a Huffman tree by hand: repeatedly take the two lowest-frequency nodes (starting with the two count-1 letters), merge them into a new node whose weight is their sum, and keep repeating until one tree remains.
Walk the finished tree to read off each letter's binary code (left branch = 0, right branch = 1, root to leaf), and write down the resulting code table.

Encode the full 11-letter string with your code table and count the total bits used; compare that against a fixed-width code (5 distinct symbols needs 3 bits each, i.e. 33 bits for 11 letters) and compute the percentage saved.

Save the same 11-character string in a plain text file, then compress that file with any zip utility, and compare the file sizes on disk — notice the saved space is far less impressive than your hand calculation, because ZIP's fixed header/metadata overhead dominates on such a tiny file, a real and common gotcha.

Pick a 3-letter word from your own name and hand-encode it in Base64 following the byte-splitting method described earlier, then check your answer with a scripting language's built-in Base64 function.

Save one photo as an uncompressed BMP, then export the same photo as a PNG and as a JPEG at medium quality from an image editor; record all three file sizes and compute each one's compression ratio relative to the BMP.

Zoom into the JPEG version at high magnification around a sharp edge in the image and look for faint square patterning — you're looking directly at the boundaries of the 8x8 blocks the DCT compression step operates on.

guides.title: Cryptography & Keeping Secrets
guides.summary: The science of protecting information: confidentiality, integrity and authentication; why classical ciphers fail; symmetric and public-key encryption with a worked RSA example; hashes, signatures and certificates; and the practical rules for storing passwords and managing keys safely.

sections.heading: The Four Goals and the Core Vocabulary
sections.body: Cryptography is the mathematical study of securing communication in the presence of adversaries, and it is worth being precise from the outset that it pursues four distinct goals which are often conflated. Confidentiality means only the intended parties can read the message. Integrity means the message has not been altered in transit, whether by accident or by deliberate tampering. Authentication means the parties are genuinely who they claim to be. Non-repudiation means a sender cannot later credibly deny having sent something. These are separable properties, and a system can achieve one while completely failing another. Encryption alone, for instance, provides confidentiality but by itself provides no integrity whatsoever: an attacker who cannot read your ciphertext may still be able to flip specific bits in it and thereby flip corresponding bits in the decrypted plaintext, changing a transferred amount or a permission flag without ever learning what the message said. That gap is the single most common design error in amateur cryptography and the reason modern practice insists on authenticated encryption rather than encryption alone. The core vocabulary is small. Plaintext is the original readable message; ciphertext is the scrambled result; encryption is the transformation from one to the other and decryption is its inverse; the cipher is the algorithm performing the transformation; and the key is the secret parameter that selects which of the algorithm's enormous family of possible transformations is actually applied. A related term, cryptanalysis, is the study of breaking these systems, and cryptology is the umbrella covering both. The organising principle of the whole field was stated by Auguste Kerckhoffs in 1883: a system must remain secure even if everything about it except the key is public knowledge. Claude Shannon restated it more bluntly as the assumption that the enemy knows the system. This is not an aesthetic preference but a hard-won engineering conclusion. Algorithms leak, through reverse engineering, through disclosure, through employees changing jobs, and an algorithm's secrecy cannot be revoked and replaced the way a key can. A system whose security rests on the algorithm staying hidden fails permanently and silently the moment it is discovered, whereas a system whose security rests on the key can recover by simply issuing a new key. Security through obscurity, meaning hoping an adversary never learns your method, is therefore treated as an anti-pattern. Real cryptography uses openly published algorithms subjected to years of adversarial peer review, precisely because surviving sustained public attack by experts is the only available evidence that something is actually hard to break. A final caution: cryptography secures data, not systems. It cannot protect against a compromised endpoint, a keylogger, a coerced user, or an attacker who simply reads the plaintext before it is ever encrypted, and it is routinely bypassed rather than broken.

sections.heading: Classical Ciphers and Why They Fail
sections.body: Early ciphers repay study because each one fails in a different instructive way. The Caesar cipher shifts every letter by a fixed amount, so with a shift of three A becomes D, B becomes E, and HELLO becomes KHOOR. Its fatal weakness is key space: there are only 25 meaningful shifts, so an attacker writes out all 25 candidate decryptions and reads the one that is English. That takes seconds by hand. The obvious fix is a general substitution cipher, in which each letter maps to an arbitrary other letter under a fixed permutation. Now the key space is 26 factorial, roughly 4 times 10 to the 26, which is far beyond brute force even for a computer. Yet a substitution cipher is broken by a schoolchild with patience, because it preserves the statistical fingerprint of the language. In ordinary English E appears about 12.7 percent of the time, followed by T at 9.1, A at 8.2 and O at 7.5, while Z and Q are under 0.1 percent. The most common ciphertext letter is therefore almost certainly E; single-letter words are A or I; the most common three-letter pattern is THE; doubled letters are usually LL, SS, EE or OO. Each guess constrains the next and the whole mapping unravels within a page of text. This is the essential lesson: a huge key space is necessary but nowhere near sufficient. The Vigenère cipher answers frequency analysis by using a repeating keyword to vary the shift by position, so the same plaintext letter encrypts differently depending on where it falls. It resisted attack for roughly three centuries and was called le chiffre indéchiffrable. Its weakness is the repetition itself. Because the key repeats every n letters, the ciphertext is really n interleaved Caesar ciphers, and the key length can be recovered. The Kasiski examination finds repeated ciphertext trigrams and takes the greatest common divisor of the distances between them, since an identical plaintext fragment aligned with an identical key fragment produces identical ciphertext. The index of coincidence measures how often two randomly chosen letters match, about 0.067 for English against 0.038 for random text, and tests candidate key lengths for the value that looks most like natural language. Once n is known, each of the n columns is attacked separately by frequency analysis. The general moral is that an intuitively strong scheme can conceal a fatal statistical structure that its designer never imagined. Modern ciphers are designed so that ciphertext is computationally indistinguishable from random noise, which by construction defeats every attack of this family. This is also the concrete reason for the standing advice never to invent your own cipher for real use: the flaw will not be visible to you.

sections.heading: Symmetric Encryption and the One-Time Pad
sections.body: Symmetric encryption, also called secret-key encryption, uses the same key to encrypt and to decrypt. The theoretically perfect member of the family is the one-time pad: combine each plaintext bit with a truly random key bit using exclusive-or, where the key is at least as long as the message and is never reused. Claude Shannon proved in 1949 that this achieves perfect secrecy, meaning the ciphertext carries literally zero information about the plaintext; for any candidate message of the same length there exists a key that would produce exactly the observed ciphertext, so an adversary with unlimited computing power learns nothing. The catch is entirely practical. The key must be as long as all traffic ever sent, must be genuinely random rather than generated by an algorithm, must be distributed securely in advance, and must never be reused. Reuse is catastrophic rather than merely weakening: exclusive-oring two ciphertexts encrypted under the same pad cancels the key entirely and yields the exclusive-or of the two plaintexts, which is readable by hand. This is not hypothetical; it is precisely how the Venona project read Soviet traffic after duplicate pad pages were issued. Real systems therefore use block ciphers. The standard is AES, the Advanced Encryption Standard, selected in 2001 from an open international competition, originally submitted as Rijndael. It encrypts 128-bit blocks under keys of 128, 192 or 256 bits through repeated rounds, 10 for AES-128, 12 for AES-192, 14 for AES-256, each round applying byte substitution, row shifting, column mixing and key addition so that every output bit depends on every input bit and every key bit. AES-256 has 2 to the 256 possible keys, roughly 10 to the 77, comparable to the number of atoms in the observable universe, so exhaustive search is not merely impractical but thermodynamically impossible. Crucially, a block cipher on its own is not an encryption scheme. Used naively in electronic codebook mode, identical plaintext blocks produce identical ciphertext blocks, so structure leaks straight through; the canonical demonstration is an image of a penguin encrypted in ECB mode, which remains perfectly recognisable. A mode of operation fixes this by chaining or randomising each block. Cipher block chaining exclusive-ors each block with the previous ciphertext and requires a random initialisation vector, but provides no integrity and is vulnerable to padding oracle attacks when misused. The modern default is Galois/Counter Mode, which turns the block cipher into a stream and simultaneously computes an authentication tag, giving confidentiality and integrity together. Its one absolute rule is that a nonce must never repeat under the same key, since nonce reuse in GCM leaks the authentication subkey and destroys both properties at once. Symmetric crypto is fast and ideal for bulk data; its single hard problem is agreeing on the key in the first place.

sections.heading: Public-Key Cryptography: RSA and Diffie–Hellman
sections.body: Public-key, or asymmetric, cryptography was published by Whitfield Diffie and Martin Hellman in 1976, and independently discovered earlier at Britain's GCHQ but kept classified until 1997. It uses a mathematically linked key pair: a public key that may be freely published, and a private key kept secret. Data encrypted with the public key can be decrypted only with the matching private key, which dissolves the key-distribution problem, because you can publish your public key on a billboard and anyone can then send you something only you can open. RSA, named for Rivest, Shamir and Adleman in 1977, rests on the asymmetry between multiplication and factoring: multiplying two large primes is trivial, while recovering them from the product is believed to be very hard. A worked toy example makes the machinery concrete, though note the numbers are absurdly small for illustration. Choose primes p equals 61 and q equals 53, so the modulus n equals 3233. Compute Euler's totient, phi of n, as 60 times 52 equals 3120. Choose a public exponent e equal to 17, which shares no factor with 3120; the public key is the pair 3233 and 17. Find the private exponent d such that d times e is congruent to 1 modulo 3120, which gives d equals 2753 via the extended Euclidean algorithm. To encrypt the message 65, compute 65 to the 17th power modulo 3233, which equals 2790. To decrypt, compute 2790 to the 2753rd power modulo 3233, recovering exactly 65. The correctness follows from Euler's theorem. An attacker sees only n and e, and recovering d requires factoring 3233 back into 61 and 53, which takes a moment by hand here and is believed infeasible for a properly generated 2048-bit modulus. Two honest caveats matter. Textbook RSA as just described is insecure in practice because it is deterministic and multiplicatively malleable; real implementations use randomised padding such as OAEP, and real signatures use PSS. And RSA is used almost exclusively to transport keys, not to encrypt data, because it is thousands of times slower than AES and can only encrypt a message shorter than the modulus. Diffie-Hellman key exchange solves the same problem differently: two parties publicly agree a generator and a prime, each picks a private exponent, each sends the generator raised to their exponent, and each raises the received value to their own exponent, arriving at the same shared secret which was never transmitted. Its security rests on the discrete logarithm problem. Plain Diffie-Hellman authenticates nobody and is trivially defeated by an active man-in-the-middle unless combined with signatures. In practice everything is hybrid: slow asymmetric crypto establishes a fast symmetric session key, which then does the actual work.

sections.heading: Hash Functions and Message Authentication
sections.body: A cryptographic hash function compresses input of any length into a fixed-size output called a digest or fingerprint; SHA-256 produces 256 bits, conventionally written as 64 hexadecimal characters. Three properties define it. It is deterministic, so the same input always yields the same digest. It is preimage resistant, meaning that given a digest it is infeasible to find any input producing it, which is what makes it one-way. And it is collision resistant, meaning it is infeasible to find two different inputs sharing a digest. A closely related and slightly weaker property, second-preimage resistance, says that given one specific input it is infeasible to find a different input with the same digest. The avalanche effect underpins all of this: changing a single input bit flips approximately half the output bits, so digests of similar inputs are entirely unrelated. Hashing the string hello with SHA-256 gives one 64-character value and hashing Hello gives a completely different one with no visible relationship. Understanding the birthday paradox is essential for judging strength. Because a collision only requires any two inputs to match rather than a match against a specific target, collision resistance offers only half the bit strength of preimage resistance: SHA-256 provides 256-bit preimage resistance but roughly 128-bit collision resistance, since finding a collision by brute force takes about 2 to the 128 operations rather than 2 to the 256. This is exactly why 128-bit digests are considered inadequate today. Typical uses are file integrity verification, where you compare a download's computed hash against a published one; deduplication and content addressing, as in Git commit identifiers and BitTorrent; and password storage, though that case demands deliberately slow specialised functions rather than a fast general hash. MD5 and SHA-1 must not be used for any security purpose. MD5 collisions were demonstrated in 2004 and can now be generated in seconds; SHA-1 fell to a practical collision in 2017 with the SHAttered attack, which produced two distinct PDF files with the same digest, and by 2020 chosen-prefix collisions made forging realistic documents feasible. Use SHA-256, SHA-512 or SHA-3. A plain hash alone proves nothing about origin, because anyone can recompute it over modified data. To prove a message came unaltered from someone holding a shared secret key, use an HMAC, a Hash-based Message Authentication Code, which mixes the key into the hash through a specific nested construction with inner and outer padding. That construction is not decorative; the naive alternative of hashing the key concatenated with the message is vulnerable to length-extension attacks against Merkle-Damgård hashes like SHA-256, letting an attacker append data and produce a valid tag without knowing the key. Always compare authentication tags with a constant-time comparison, since a byte-by-byte comparison that returns early leaks the correct tag through timing.

sections.heading: Digital Signatures, Certificates and TLS
sections.body: A digital signature inverts the public-key roles to prove authorship and integrity rather than to provide secrecy. The signer computes a hash of the document and transforms that hash with their private key; anyone can apply the corresponding public key and compare the result against their own independently computed hash of the document. A match establishes that the document is unaltered, since any change would produce a different hash, and that it came from the holder of the private key, which gives authentication and, given adequate key protection and legal framework, non-repudiation. Signing the hash rather than the document itself is both an efficiency measure and a security requirement, since the transformation operates on a fixed small input. Describing RSA signing as encrypting with the private key is a common simplification that is close enough for intuition but technically wrong for modern schemes, which use distinct padding constructions such as PSS, and entirely inapplicable to ECDSA and Ed25519 where signing and encryption are structurally different operations. This raises the harder question: how do you know a public key genuinely belongs to the person or website claiming it? The answer is a Public Key Infrastructure. A Certificate Authority signs a certificate binding an identity to a public key, and your browser or operating system ships with a preinstalled set of trusted root CAs against which certificate chains are validated. This underpins HTTPS through TLS, Transport Layer Security. A simplified TLS 1.3 handshake runs as follows: the client sends supported cipher suites together with its ephemeral Diffie-Hellman key share; the server replies with its own key share, its certificate, and a signature over the handshake transcript made with the private key corresponding to that certificate; the client validates the certificate chain to a trusted root, checks the name matches, checks validity dates and revocation, and verifies the signature; both sides then derive a shared symmetric key and all subsequent traffic is protected with a fast authenticated cipher such as AES-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305. TLS 1.3 completes this in a single round trip and removed the older versions' insecure options. Two caveats are worth stating plainly. The padlock icon means the connection is encrypted and the server proved control of that domain name; it does not mean the site is honest, and phishing sites routinely obtain valid certificates. And the CA model is only as strong as its weakest member, since any of hundreds of trusted CAs can technically issue a certificate for any domain; the DigiNotar compromise in 2011 produced fraudulent Google certificates used to intercept Iranian users' traffic. Certificate Transparency logs, which publish every issued certificate to append-only public logs so that unauthorised issuance for your domain becomes detectable, and certificate pinning, which binds a client to a specific expected key, exist precisely to constrain that risk. A related property worth understanding is forward secrecy: because TLS 1.3 derives session keys from ephemeral Diffie-Hellman values discarded after the handshake, an adversary who records traffic today and later obtains the server's long-term private key still cannot decrypt those recordings.

sections.heading: Passwords, Key Management and Randomness
sections.body: The overwhelming majority of real-world breaches exploit key and password handling rather than broken mathematics, so this is where practical effort belongs. Passwords must never be stored as plaintext, and equally must never be stored as a plain fast hash such as SHA-256, because a modern GPU computes billions of SHA-256 hashes per second and will exhaust any realistic human password. Use a deliberately slow, salted, memory-hard password hashing function: Argon2id is the current recommendation, with scrypt and bcrypt remaining acceptable and PBKDF2 acceptable only where nothing better is available. A salt is a unique random value, typically 16 bytes, generated per password and stored alongside the hash; it is not secret. Its purpose is to ensure two users with the same password produce different hashes, which defeats precomputed rainbow tables and forces an attacker to attack each account separately rather than the whole database at once. A pepper, by contrast, is a secret value shared across all passwords and stored separately from the database, offering additional protection specifically when the database alone leaks. Cost parameters should be tuned so a single verification takes on the order of 100 to 500 milliseconds on your production hardware, which is imperceptible to a legitimate user and multiplies an attacker's cost by many orders of magnitude. Argon2id's memory parameter matters independently, because forcing each guess to occupy tens of megabytes destroys the parallelism advantage of GPUs and custom hardware. Randomness is the other recurring failure. Keys, salts, nonces and initialisation vectors must come from a cryptographically secure pseudo-random number generator seeded from the operating system entropy pool, meaning /dev/urandom, getrandom, or the language's dedicated secure API, never a general-purpose rand or a Mersenne Twister, whose entire internal state can be reconstructed from a few hundred outputs. Weak randomness has broken real systems repeatedly: a Debian OpenSSL packaging error in 2008 reduced the key space to a few tens of thousands of possibilities, and Sony's PlayStation 3 signing key was recovered in 2010 because the ECDSA implementation reused a fixed nonce, which mathematically reveals the private key from two signatures. Never reuse a key, nonce or pad. Key sizes should meet current guidance: AES-128 is adequate and AES-256 preferred, RSA and Diffie-Hellman at 2048 bits minimum with 3072 preferred for long-term data, and elliptic curves at 256 bits, where P-256 or Curve25519 give roughly the same strength as RSA-3072 in a fraction of the size. Protect private keys at rest in a hardware security module, a smartcard or a phone's secure enclave, so the key performs operations without ever being extractable. Rotate keys on a schedule, and design so that rotation is routine rather than an emergency.

sections.heading: Common Mistakes and Safe Practice
sections.body: A short catalogue of recurring failures is more useful than any amount of theory, because these are the errors that actually appear in production code. Rolling your own crypto is first, and the point is not that the mathematics is beyond you but that a cipher can be functionally correct, pass every test, and still leak the key through a timing side channel or a padding oracle. Use audited libraries and standards: libsodium, the platform's own cryptographic API, TLS 1.3, AES-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305. Second, confusing encoding with encryption. Base64, hexadecimal and URL encoding are reversible transformations with no key and provide precisely zero secrecy; obfuscation is not protection. Third, using broken primitives. MD5 and SHA-1 have practical collisions, DES has a 56-bit key breakable in hours, RC4 has exploitable biases, and ECB mode leaks plaintext structure. Fourth, hardcoding secrets. Keys committed to source control leak constantly, and because version history is permanent, deleting the line later does not remove the secret; automated scanners harvest public repositories for exposed credentials within minutes of a push. Fifth, ignoring integrity. Encryption without authentication permits undetected tampering, so always use authenticated encryption or apply an HMAC, and where you build the combination yourself, encrypt first and then authenticate the ciphertext rather than the reverse. Sixth, poor key exchange, meaning transmitting a symmetric key alongside the data it protects, which defeats the entire construction. Seventh, overtrusting: disabling certificate validation to make development work and shipping it, or training users to dismiss browser warnings. Two further items deserve mention because they are less obvious. Timing side channels arise when the time taken to process data depends on secret values, so comparisons of authentication tags, MACs and passwords must run in constant time. And error messages that distinguish between failure modes create oracles; the classic padding oracle attack recovers entire plaintexts using nothing but a server that reports padding errors differently from authentication errors. Looking forward, a sufficiently large fault-tolerant quantum computer would break RSA, Diffie-Hellman and elliptic-curve cryptography via Shor's algorithm, which factors and computes discrete logarithms in polynomial time. Symmetric cryptography is far less affected: Grover's algorithm gives only a square-root speedup, so AES-256 retains roughly 128-bit security and doubling key length suffices. NIST standardised the first post-quantum algorithms in 2024, including ML-KEM for key encapsulation and ML-DSA for signatures, and hybrid deployments combining classical and post-quantum key exchange are already shipping, motivated by harvest-now-decrypt-later attacks against data that must stay secret for decades. One further practical rule deserves stating: cryptography protects data in transit and at rest, but it cannot protect data in use, so an attacker with code execution on the endpoint reads the plaintext before it is encrypted or after it is decrypted, and no cipher choice changes that. This is why serious systems pair cryptography with hardware-backed key storage, least-privilege access and logging rather than treating encryption as a sufficient control on its own. The enduring principle is unchanged: keep the key secret, use vetted public algorithms, always authenticate, and generate keys with strong randomness. The mathematics is only ever as strong as the operational discipline surrounding it.

sections.heading: Elliptic-Curve Cryptography: Smaller Keys, Same Strength
sections.body: RSA and Diffie-Hellman both lean on a single family of hard problems: given a huge number, either factor it, or compute a discrete logarithm in the integers modulo a prime. Elliptic-curve cryptography obtains the same public-key capabilities, key exchange and digital signatures, from a different hard problem that permits dramatically smaller numbers for equivalent security. An elliptic curve here is the set of points satisfying an equation of the form y squared equals x cubed plus ax plus b, evaluated over a finite field, meaning arithmetic modulo a large prime, so the curve is a finite scatter of discrete points rather than a smooth continuous shape, together with one special point at infinity acting as the identity element. These points support a defined addition operation: the line through two points on the curve meets it at a third point, whose reflection across the x axis is defined as the sum, with a tangent line used when adding a point to itself. Repeating that addition, computing kP meaning P added to itself k times, is called scalar multiplication and is performed efficiently by double-and-add in a number of steps proportional to the bit length of k, playing exactly the role modular exponentiation plays in RSA. The elliptic-curve discrete logarithm problem is then: given P and Q equals kP, recover k. Unlike integer factoring, for which the general number field sieve provides a sub-exponential algorithm, no sub-exponential attack is publicly known against a well-chosen curve. The best general method, Pollard's rho, runs in time proportional to the square root of the group order, which remains fully exponential in the key length. That asymmetry in attack complexity is the entire source of the size advantage: a 256-bit elliptic-curve key delivers roughly the security of a 3072-bit RSA key, both landing near 128-bit symmetric-equivalent strength under NIST's comparable-strength tables, and a 384-bit curve corresponds to a 7680-bit RSA modulus. Smaller keys mean smaller certificates, shorter handshakes, less bandwidth and far less computation, savings that matter enormously on battery-powered phones and constrained embedded devices. This is why TLS 1.3 defaults its key exchange to X25519, a curve designed by Daniel J. Bernstein specifically for speed and for resistance to implementation mistakes, and why Ed25519 is now a common default for SSH keys and underlies signatures in the Signal protocol. Two honest caveats. Curve choice is load-bearing rather than cosmetic; some curves have special structure that weakens them, some standardised curves attracted suspicion over unexplained parameter selection, and the Curve25519 family was designed partly to make constant-time, exception-free implementation the natural outcome rather than a careful achievement. And ECC's size advantage does not survive quantum computing: Shor's algorithm breaks elliptic-curve discrete logarithms as readily as it breaks factoring, and smaller keys mean a quantum attacker needs fewer logical qubits, so ECC is if anything the earlier casualty rather than the safer refuge.

sections.heading: Breaking Enigma: A Real Lesson in Why Key Space Isn't Enough
sections.body: It is tempting to treat cryptographic security as purely a numbers game, on the assumption that a large enough key space guarantees safety. The wartime breaking of the German Enigma is the clearest historical demonstration that this is false. Enigma was an electromechanical cipher machine: the operator pressed a letter key, current flowed through a plugboard that swapped pairs of letters, then through three or four rotors each performing its own substitution and stepping like an odometer with every keypress so the substitution changed letter by letter, then through a reflector that sent the current back through the rotors a second time before illuminating an output lamp. With rotor selection and order, ring settings, starting positions and plugboard wiring all forming part of the daily key, the number of possible settings on a wartime military Enigma was on the order of 10 to the 23, and the plugboard alone with ten cables contributed roughly 150 trillion combinations. Naively that is unsearchable with 1940s technology, and the German command believed exactly that. It was broken anyway. Marian Rejewski of the Polish Cipher Bureau reconstructed the internal rotor wiring mathematically in the early 1930s using permutation group theory, exploiting the German practice of sending each message's key twice at the start, and aided by documents obtained through French intelligence. Poland handed this work to Britain and France in July 1939, weeks before the war began. At Bletchley Park, Alan Turing and Gordon Welchman built on the Polish bomba to construct the Bombe, a machine that never searched the key space at all. It exploited how Enigma was actually used. The reflector introduced a structural flaw: because current always returned through the rotors, no letter could ever encipher to itself. Combined with cribs, meaning guessed plaintext from stereotyped weather reports, routine sign-offs, the word Keine, or phrases operators repeated out of habit, that single constraint let the Bombe test a crib against candidate rotor settings and reject the overwhelming majority mechanically through contradiction, reducing a hopeless search to a handful of settings for hand checking each day. Welchman's diagonal board multiplied the elimination rate further. Operator discipline failures compounded it: reused indicator settings, predictable three-letter keys such as initials, and messages sent in both Enigma and a weaker cipher. The lesson generalises directly. Attackers essentially never brute-force a well-designed modern cipher's key space, since AES-256's 2 to the 256 possibilities remain, as far as anyone publicly knows, beyond any computer that will ever be built. Real breaks come from protocol misuse, implementation bugs, side channels, predictable or reused keys, and operational shortcuts. Enigma's key space was never the weak point; its usage was, and the same is true of essentially every system compromised since.

sections.heading: Equipment You'll Actually Need
sections.body: Cryptography is unusual among practical subjects in that it requires almost no equipment: the whole discipline is arithmetic, and a machine that can multiply large numbers and read a file is a complete laboratory. What the items gathered here are for is making the abstractions tangible, because there is a substantial difference between reading that a hash is deterministic and one-way and watching two nearly identical files produce two completely unrelated 64-character digests on your own screen. A terminal with a scripting language or a general-purpose cryptographic command-line toolkit matters specifically because both let you observe intermediate values, which graphical tools deliberately hide; you want to see the actual certificate fields, the actual modulus, the actual tag, not a green padlock. Modular exponentiation deserves its own tool because doing it by naive repeated multiplication overflows any calculator almost immediately: computing 65 to the 17th power before reducing produces a 31-digit number, whereas reducing modulo n after every squaring keeps every intermediate value under four digits. That single insight, that you reduce as you go rather than at the end, is why RSA is computable at all, and it is best learned by hitting the overflow once. Pen and paper remain genuinely useful for the extended Euclidean algorithm, which is the one step people reliably fumble when they only ever call a library function for it. Inspecting a real certificate in a browser is worth more than any diagram of a public key infrastructure, because you see the actual issuer chain, the validity window, the signature algorithm and the subject alternative names, and you discover how short a modern certificate's lifetime has become. A shuffled deck is included for a specific reason: entropy is the least intuitive concept in the field, and physically producing about 226 bits of it, then comparing that against a seeded software generator that reproduces the same sequence every run, makes the distinction between random and merely unpredictable-looking concrete in a way no definition manages.
ingredients: A computer with a terminal and either Python (using its built-in hashlib module, or a widely available third-party cryptography library) or the OpenSSL command-line toolkit (a free, widely used cryptography utility, often already installed on macOS/Linux and freely downloadable for Windows)
A calculator capable of modular exponentiation, or a spreadsheet program set up to compute it step by step, for working through RSA arithmetic without errors
Pen and paper for practicing modular arithmetic and prime factorization by hand
A web browser, used to click the padlock/site-information icon on any HTTPS website you already visit and inspect its real certificate chain, issuer and expiry date firsthand

A deck of playing cards, useful for generating genuine physical randomness (a well-shuffled 52-card deck carries roughly 226 bits of entropy) to compare against a computer's pseudo-random number generator
Optional: a classical cipher wheel or similar puzzle toy (sold as an educational/puzzle item) for hands-on practice with substitution and shift ciphers before moving to the software exercises

sections.heading: Step-by-Step: Crack a Caesar Cipher and Build Tiny RSA by Hand
sections.body: These two exercises are chosen because they teach opposite halves of the subject. Attacking a Caesar cipher by frequency analysis demonstrates that structure in the plaintext survives a naive transformation and can be recovered statistically, which is the single most important intuition in cryptanalysis and the reason modern ciphertext is engineered to look like noise. Building a working RSA key pair by hand demonstrates the opposite: that security can rest on a computational asymmetry rather than on hiding a method, since every value except the private exponent is published and the system still holds. Do the arithmetic yourself rather than reading it, because two specific realisations only arrive through doing. The first is that modular reduction must happen at every squaring step or the intermediate numbers explode beyond any calculator. The second is how uncomfortably fast the toy modulus factors, which makes the leap to 2048-bit primes feel like a quantitative rather than a qualitative safeguard, which is exactly what it is.
steps: Write a short English sentence and encrypt it yourself using a Caesar shift of 7 (replace every letter with the one 7 positions later in the alphabet, wrapping Z back to A).

Set the ciphertext aside, then attack it as if you didn't know the key: count how often each letter appears, and note which letter appears most — in ordinary English text 'E' is by far the most common letter, so the most frequent ciphertext letter is a strong first guess for what 'E' was shifted to.

Use that guess to compute the likely shift value, apply it to decrypt the whole message, and check whether the result is coherent English; if not, try the second- or third-most-frequent letter as your guess for 'E' and repeat.
Now build a small working RSA key pair by hand. Choose two small prime numbers, p=61 and q=53 (small enough for hand or calculator arithmetic, though far too small for real security).
Compute n = p x q = 3233 (this becomes your public modulus) and phi(n) = (p-1) x (q-1) = 60 x 52 = 3120.
Choose a public exponent e that shares no common factors with 3120 — e=17 works (3120's prime factors are 2, 3, 5; 17 shares none of them).
Find the private exponent d, the modular inverse of e mod phi(n), using the extended Euclidean algorithm by hand or a calculator — for these numbers, d=2753.
Encrypt a small test message, e.g. m=65, by computing c = m^e mod n via repeated squaring (a calculator with a mod-exponentiation function makes this fast) — you should get c=2790.
Decrypt it back with m = c^d mod n and confirm you recover 65 exactly, proving the key pair works.

Reflect on scale: n=3233 factors trivially by hand in seconds (61 x 53) — real RSA uses primes hundreds of digits long specifically so this factoring step becomes computationally infeasible; this exercise is for understanding the mechanism only, never for anything you'd actually want kept secret.

guides.title: Formal Logic & Clear Reasoning
guides.summary: The rules of valid inference: propositions and truth tables, logical equivalences like De Morgan's laws, the difference between validity and truth, quantifiers, rigorous proof techniques including induction, and the common fallacies to avoid — the shared foundation of mathematics, programming and clear thinking.

sections.heading: Propositions, Connectives and Truth Tables
sections.body: Formal logic studies the structure of valid reasoning independently of subject matter, which is why the same rules govern a mathematical proof, a legal argument and a line of program code. Its atom is the proposition: a declarative statement that is either true (T) or false (F) and never both. 'It is raining' is a proposition because it has a definite truth value even if you do not currently know which. 'Close the door' is a command and 'x + 1' is an expression with no truth value, so neither qualifies. Propositions are combined using logical connectives, and the whole discipline rests on the fact that each connective is defined by nothing more than how it maps input truth values onto an output. Negation, written NOT P or with the hook symbol, simply reverses truth, so not-true is false. Conjunction, written P AND Q, is true only when both parts are true. Disjunction, written P OR Q, is true when at least one part is true; this is the inclusive or, so it remains true when both hold, which is the opposite of the exclusive 'or' of everyday speech in a phrase like 'soup or salad'. The conditional, written IF P THEN P implies Q, is the one that trips people up: it is false in exactly one case, when P is true and Q is false, and true in every other case including every case where P is false. A conditional with a false antecedent is called vacuously true, so the sentence 'if the moon is made of cheese then I am the king of Spain' counts as true in formal logic. P is called the antecedent and Q the consequent. The biconditional, P if and only if Q, is true whenever both sides carry the same truth value. A truth table makes all of this mechanical: it enumerates every possible combination of the component propositions and records the resulting value of the whole expression. For n distinct propositions there are exactly two-to-the-n rows, so two propositions need four rows, three need eight, and five already need thirty-two, which is roughly where hand construction stops being practical and errors creep in. Truth tables are the ground truth of propositional logic in a strong sense: any question about a compound statement, including whether two statements mean the same thing or whether an argument is valid, can in principle be settled by building the table and reading it. The one honest caveat is cost. Deciding satisfiability by exhaustive table is exponential in the number of variables, which is why real tools use smarter search. These same tables are identical to the behaviour of hardware logic gates, so the discipline is genuinely the same whether it is being done by a philosopher with chalk or by silicon switching at a billion times a second.

sections.heading: Logical Equivalences and the Laws of Logic
sections.body: Two statements are logically equivalent, written with a triple-bar symbol, when they have identical truth tables. This is a far stronger claim than saying they happen to agree in the current situation. It means they come out the same in every possible situation, which is precisely what licenses you to substitute one for the other anywhere, in a proof, in a database query or in a compiler optimisation, without changing meaning. A small set of laws does nearly all the work. Double negation says that not-not-P is just P. The commutative laws say that order does not matter for AND or for OR, so P AND Q means the same as Q AND P. The associative laws say that grouping does not matter when the same connective repeats, so bracketing three ANDs either way gives the same result. The distributive laws let one connective be pushed through another, so P AND the quantity Q OR R equals the quantity P AND Q, OR the quantity P AND R, exactly mirroring how multiplication distributes over addition in arithmetic. De Morgan's laws are the two most useful in practice: the negation of a conjunction equals the disjunction of the negations, and the negation of a disjunction equals the conjunction of the negations. In plain words, 'not both A and B' means 'either not-A or not-B', while 'neither A nor B' means 'not-A and also not-B'. Concretely, the negation of 'the door is locked and the alarm is on' is not 'the door is unlocked and the alarm is off'; it is 'the door is unlocked or the alarm is off', because only one of the two needs to fail for the conjunction to be false. Getting this wrong is one of the most common bugs in both written arguments and in code. The contrapositive law states that a conditional and its contrapositive are always equivalent: if P then Q means exactly the same as if not-Q then not-P. This single equivalence powers an entire proof method, because it lets you attack a statement from whichever end is easier. It must not be confused with the converse, if Q then P, which is a genuinely different statement, nor with the inverse, if not-P then not-Q. Finally, a conditional can always be rewritten as a disjunction: if P then Q equals not-P or Q, which is how compilers and theorem provers normalise conditionals away entirely. A statement that comes out true on every row of its table, whatever its parts do, is a tautology, the standard example being P or not-P, the law of excluded middle. A statement false on every row is a contradiction, such as P and not-P. Everything else is contingent. These laws are applied constantly to simplify program conditionals, shrink digital circuits and rewrite search filters into faster equivalent forms.

sections.heading: Arguments: Validity, Soundness and Inference Rules
sections.body: An argument consists of one or more premises, which are statements taken as given, and a conclusion said to follow from them. The single most important distinction in the whole subject is between validity and soundness, and confusing the two produces endless bad debate. An argument is valid when the conclusion must be true in every situation where all the premises are true. Validity is purely a property of form and says nothing whatever about whether the premises are actually true. 'All fish can fly; a salmon is a fish; therefore a salmon can fly' is a perfectly valid argument with a false conclusion, because its first premise is false. An argument is sound when it is valid and its premises are in fact true, and only soundness guarantees a true conclusion. When you disagree with someone's conclusion, this tells you there are exactly two places to attack: the form, or the premises. Several argument forms are guaranteed valid and are worth memorising as reflexes. Modus ponens goes from 'if P then Q' together with P, to Q: if rain implies the ground is wet, and it is raining, then the ground is wet. Modus tollens goes from 'if P then Q' together with not-Q, to not-P: if rain implies the ground is wet, and the ground is not wet, then it did not rain. Hypothetical syllogism chains conditionals, so from 'if P then Q' and 'if Q then R' you get 'if P then R'. Disjunctive syllogism eliminates an option, so from 'P or Q' and not-P you get Q. Each of these can be verified mechanically by building the truth table and confirming that no row has all premises true with the conclusion false. Set against these are two invalid look-alikes that are responsible for a large share of everyday reasoning errors. Affirming the consequent argues from 'if P then Q' and Q to P, which fails because the ground could be wet from a sprinkler, a burst pipe or a street cleaner. Denying the antecedent argues from 'if P then Q' and not-P to not-Q, which fails for the same reason in mirror image. Both feel persuasive because English often uses 'if' loosely to mean 'if and only if', and under a genuine biconditional both patterns would in fact be valid; the fallacy lies in silently upgrading a one-way conditional into a two-way one. Finally, everything described here is deductive reasoning, in which a valid form guarantees the conclusion. Inductive reasoning, which generalises from observed examples, offers only probability: a thousand white swans support but never prove that all swans are white, and a single black one overturns it. Science runs on induction disciplined by attempts at refutation, while mathematics runs on deduction, and treating one as the other is a category error.

sections.heading: Predicate Logic and Quantifiers
sections.body: Propositional logic treats each statement as an indivisible unit, which means it cannot see inside a sentence and therefore cannot express anything about 'all' or 'some'. It has no way to record that 'Socrates is a man' and 'all men are mortal' share the concept of being a man, so it cannot derive that Socrates is mortal. Predicate logic, also called first-order logic, fixes this by adding two ingredients: predicates and quantifiers. A predicate is a property or a relation with one or more slots, and it only becomes a proposition once every slot is filled. Written Prime(x), the expression 'x is prime' is neither true nor false until x is specified; Prime(7) is true and Prime(8) is false. Relations take several slots, so Loves(a, b) or GreaterThan(x, y) express links between things rather than properties of one thing. Quantifiers bind the free variables over a stated domain of discourse, and naming that domain is not optional bureaucracy: 'every number has a successor' is true over the integers and false over a finite set, so the same formula changes truth value when the domain changes. The universal quantifier, read 'for all', asserts that a predicate holds of every element of the domain, and it is disproved by producing a single counterexample. The existential quantifier, read 'there exists', asserts that the predicate holds of at least one element, and it is proved by producing a single witness. This asymmetry is practically important: universal claims are cheap to refute and expensive to establish, existential claims are the reverse. Translation follows two reliable patterns. A universal statement about a restricted group uses a conditional inside, so 'every student passed' becomes 'for all x, if x is a student then x passed'. An existential statement about a restricted group uses a conjunction inside, so 'some student failed' becomes 'there exists an x such that x is a student and x did not pass'. Mixing these up, by writing a conditional under an existential, produces a formula that is trivially satisfied by any non-student and therefore says nothing. Negation of quantifiers generalises De Morgan's laws: the negation of 'for all x, P(x)' is 'there exists an x with not-P(x)', and the negation of 'there exists an x with P(x)' is 'for all x, not-P(x)'. So 'not everyone passed' means exactly 'someone did not pass', which is a much weaker claim than 'nobody passed'. Quantifier order also carries real meaning and cannot be swapped freely. 'For all x there exists a y such that y loves x' says everyone is loved by somebody, possibly a different somebody each time, whereas 'there exists a y such that for all x, y loves x' says one particular individual loves everybody. Predicate logic in this form is the working language of mathematics, of relational database queries, and of the pre-conditions and post-conditions used to specify what a program is supposed to do.

sections.heading: Proof Techniques
sections.body: A proof is a chain of valid inferences leading from accepted premises, meaning axioms and previously established theorems, to a conclusion, with no gaps that a determined sceptic could widen. Four methods cover the great majority of ordinary mathematics, and knowing which to reach for is most of the skill. A direct proof assumes the hypothesis and works forward. To show that if n is even then n squared is even, write n as two times some integer k, which is the definition of even; then n squared equals four k squared, which equals two times the quantity two k squared, and since two k squared is an integer the result is two times an integer, hence even. Notice that the proof turns entirely on unfolding a definition, which is the usual first move when a direct attempt stalls. A proof by contrapositive replaces the goal 'if P then Q' with the logically equivalent goal 'if not-Q then not-P', which is often far easier because the new hypothesis is more concrete. To show that if n squared is even then n is even, the direct route gives you almost nothing to grip, whereas the contrapositive asks you to show that an odd n has an odd square: write n as two k plus one, square it to get four k squared plus four k plus one, which is two times the quantity two k squared plus two k, plus one, and is therefore odd. A proof by contradiction assumes the statement is false and derives an impossibility, so the assumption must be rejected. The classic case is the irrationality of the square root of two. Assume it equals a over b in lowest terms; squaring and rearranging gives two b squared equals a squared, so a squared is even, so a is even, so write a as two c; substituting gives two b squared equals four c squared, so b squared equals two c squared, so b is even as well. But then a and b share the factor two, contradicting the stipulation that the fraction was in lowest terms. A proof by induction establishes a statement for every natural number using two steps: a base case, usually n equals one, and an inductive step showing that if the statement holds for some k then it holds for k plus one. To prove that the sum of the first n whole numbers equals n times n plus one, all over two, the base case gives one equals one times two over two, which checks. Assuming the formula for k, the sum to k plus one is k times k plus one over two, plus k plus one, which factors to k plus one times k plus two, over two, exactly the formula with k plus one substituted. The most common error is a missing or unverified base case, which can appear to prove nonsense. Induction is the logical backbone of reasoning about loops and recursion, where the inductive hypothesis becomes a loop invariant.

sections.heading: Common Logical Fallacies
sections.body: A fallacy is a recurring error in reasoning that makes an argument invalid, or at least far weaker than it appears. Learning to name them sharpens your own thinking and gives you a defence against manipulation, but the naming is only the beginning of a response, never the whole of it. An ad hominem attacks the person rather than the argument, as in dismissing a claim because its author lacks a credential; the claim's truth does not depend on who voiced it. A straw man restates an opponent's position in a weaker or more extreme form and then refutes that instead, which is why accurately summarising a view before disagreeing with it is such a reliable signal of good faith.
